subject: physics
question_text: An angle measured in radians has a unit, yet it is called a dimensionless quantity. How can something have a unit but no dimensions?
_answer: A radian is a ratio of two lengths (arc/radius), so the length dimensions cancel; the unit 'radian' is just a label for the ratio.
_explanation: An angle in radians is defined as arc length divided by radius, so its dimensional formula is L/L = 1, meaning it is dimensionless. The name 'radian' is kept purely as a bookkeeping unit to indicate how the ratio was measured, not because it carries any physical dimension.

subject: physics
question_text: You can multiply a velocity by a time, but you can never add a velocity to a time. Why does physics allow one operation and forbid the other?
_answer: Addition requires quantities of the same dimensions (homogeneity), while multiplication simply defines a new physical quantity with combined dimensions.
_explanation: Adding quantities only makes sense if they represent the same kind of physical thing, so both terms must share dimensions. Multiplication, in contrast, creates a new quantity whose dimensions are the product of the originals — velocity times time gives displacement, a perfectly meaningful new quantity.

subject: physics
question_text: A student writes a rod's length as 2.0 cm; another writes the same rod's length as 2.00 cm. Numerically these are equal, so is there any physical difference between the two statements?
_answer: Yes — 2.00 cm claims greater precision; it has three significant figures (uncertainty ~0.01 cm) versus two for 2.0 cm (uncertainty ~0.1 cm).
_explanation: Significant figures encode the precision of a measurement. Writing 2.00 cm implies the instrument could resolve hundredths of a centimetre, while 2.0 cm implies only tenths, so the two statements make different claims about measurement uncertainty even though the numbers are equal.

subject: physics
question_text: A ball thrown straight up is momentarily at rest at the top of its flight. At that instant its velocity is zero — is its acceleration also zero?
_answer: No — acceleration is still g (about 9.8 m/s²) downward; velocity being zero at an instant does not mean it is not changing.
_explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and at the top the velocity is changing from upward to downward, passing through zero. Gravity acts throughout the flight, so the acceleration remains g downward even at the instant of momentary rest — if it were zero, the ball would stay suspended.

subject: physics
question_text: A jogger runs from home to a park and back home in one hour. Can her average speed be nonzero while her average velocity is exactly zero?
_answer: Yes — displacement for the round trip is zero, so average velocity is zero, but the path length is nonzero, so average speed is positive.
_explanation: Average velocity depends on net displacement, which vanishes when the start and end points coincide. Average speed depends on total distance travelled along the path, which is clearly nonzero for a round trip, so the two quantities can disagree dramatically.

subject: physics
question_text: An object has negative acceleration. Students often say it must be slowing down. Is that necessarily true?
_concept: sign of acceleration vs speeding up/slowing down
_answer: No — if velocity is also negative (motion in the negative direction), negative acceleration increases the speed.
_explanation: Whether an object speeds up or slows down depends on whether velocity and acceleration point the same way, not on the sign of acceleration alone. A ball falling downward with downward (negative) velocity and negative acceleration is speeding up, not slowing down.

subject: physics
question_text: At the highest point of a projectile's flight, what is the angle between its velocity and its acceleration, and why is neither of them zero there?
_concept: velocity and acceleration at the top of projectile motion
_answer: They are perpendicular (90°): velocity is purely horizontal (the horizontal component never vanished) and acceleration is g vertically downward throughout.
_explanation: Gravity only removes the vertical component of velocity, so at the peak the horizontal component remains and the velocity points horizontally. The acceleration is g downward at every instant of flight, so at the top the two vectors are exactly perpendicular.

subject: physics
question_text: Two identical balls are launched with the same speed, one at 30° and one at 60° above the horizontal. They land the same distance away. What is different about their flights?
_answer: Their ranges are equal because the angles are complementary, but the 60° ball flies higher and stays in the air longer than the 30° ball.
_explanation: Range depends on sin(2θ), and sin(60°) = sin(120°), so complementary launch angles give identical range. Maximum height and time of flight depend on the vertical velocity component sinθ, which is larger for 60°, so that trajectory is taller and slower.

subject: physics
question_text: A stone whirled in a horizontal circle at perfectly constant speed is nevertheless accelerating the whole time. How can something accelerate without changing speed?
_concept: centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion
_answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector; in circular motion the direction of velocity changes continuously, requiring a centripetal acceleration v²/r toward the centre.
_explanation: Velocity is a vector, so a change in direction alone counts as acceleration even if the magnitude stays fixed. In uniform circular motion the velocity vector constantly turns, and the acceleration responsible points toward the centre of the circle with magnitude v²/r.

subject: physics
question_text: When you walk forward, your feet push backward on the ground. What force actually propels your body forward, and where does it come from?
_concept: friction as the driving force in walking
_answer: The forward force is friction exerted by the ground on your foot — the reaction to your foot pushing backward on the ground.
_explanation: By Newton's third law, when your foot pushes the ground backward, the ground pushes your foot forward with an equal force, and this force is static friction. That is why walking is nearly impossible on frictionless ice: the ground cannot supply the forward reaction.

subject: physics
question_text: Newton's third law says every action has an equal and opposite reaction. If the forces are always equal and opposite, why don't they simply cancel out, making all motion impossible?
_concept: action-reaction pairs act on different bodies
_answer: Action and reaction act on two different bodies, so they can never cancel each other; only forces acting on the same body can cancel.
_explanation: When you push a cart, your force acts on the cart while the cart's reaction acts on you. Since each body's motion is decided only by the forces acting on that body, the pair never appears in the same equation of motion and cannot cancel.

subject: physics
question_text: A person stands on a weighing scale inside a lift whose cable has snapped so the lift is in free fall. What does the scale read, and why?
_concept: apparent weight and weightlessness in free fall
_answer: Zero — both the person and the scale accelerate downward at g, so the scale exerts (and receives) no normal force.
_explanation: A scale reads the normal contact force, not gravity directly. In free fall the person needs no supporting force to accelerate at g, so the normal force between feet and scale drops to zero and the person feels weightless.

subject: physics
question_text: When a rifle is fired, the bullet flies forward and the rifle kicks backward. The same magnitude of momentum is given to each — so why does the bullet do so much more damage than the recoiling rifle?
_concept: momentum conservation and kinetic energy distribution in recoil
_answer: Momenta are equal in magnitude, but kinetic energy (p²/2m) is far larger for the light bullet because energy at fixed momentum is inversely proportional to mass.
_explanation: Conservation of momentum forces bullet and rifle to receive equal and opposite momentum. Since kinetic energy equals p²/2m, the small-mass bullet carries almost all the energy, while the heavy rifle moves slowly with comparatively little energy.

subject: physics
question_text: A stone tied to a string moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed. The string tension constantly pulls on the stone, yet does zero work on it over any part of the motion. How?
_answer: The tension is always perpendicular to the stone's displacement, and work equals force times displacement times cos(90°) = 0.
_explanation: Work is done only by the component of force along the displacement. A centripetal force points toward the centre while the velocity is tangential, so the angle between them is always 90° and no energy is transferred — which is exactly why the speed stays constant.

subject: physics
question_text: A porter carries a heavy suitcase on his head and walks at constant velocity along a level platform. In the physics sense, how much work does he do on the suitcase, and why does the answer feel wrong?
_concept: work requires force component along displacement
_answer: Ideally zero — the supporting force is vertical while the displacement is horizontal, so W = Fd cos90° = 0, even though he tires because his muscles consume energy internally.
_explanation: Mechanical work needs a force component along the motion; here the force on the suitcase is vertical and motion is horizontal, giving zero work. The porter's fatigue comes from physiological energy spent in muscle fibres continuously contracting, which is not work done on the suitcase.

subject: physics
question_text: Potential energy of a system can be negative, but kinetic energy of a body can never be negative. What is fundamentally different about the two?
_concept: sign of kinetic vs potential energy
_answer: Kinetic energy ½mv² depends on the square of speed, which is never negative; potential energy is measured from an arbitrary reference level, so its sign depends on the chosen zero.
_explanation: Because v² is always non-negative and mass is positive, kinetic energy is intrinsically non-negative. Potential energy has no absolute zero — only differences matter — so choosing the reference at infinity, for example, makes bound gravitational systems have negative potential energy.

subject: physics
question_text: Friction is usually called a spoiler that wastes energy. Yet when a box rests on the floor of a truck that accelerates forward without the box slipping, friction on the box does positive work. Explain this.
_concept: static friction can do positive work
_answer: Static friction from the truck floor is the only horizontal force on the box; it points forward and the box moves forward, so friction does positive work, increasing the box's kinetic energy.
_explanation: There is no rule that friction must oppose motion of the body — it opposes relative slipping between surfaces. Here static friction acts forward on the box to accelerate it along with the truck, and since force and displacement are parallel, the work done is positive.

subject: physics
question_text: An ice skater spinning with arms outstretched pulls her arms in and suddenly spins much faster, with more kinetic energy than before. No one pushed her — where did the extra kinetic energy come from?
_chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
_concept: conservation of angular momentum and work done by internal forces
_answer: Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved, so reducing I raises ω; the extra kinetic energy comes from work her muscles do pulling her arms inward against the tendency to fly outward.
_explanation: With no external torque, Iω stays constant, so shrinking the moment of inertia forces the angular speed up. Rotational kinetic energy L²/2I therefore increases, and that increase is supplied by muscular work done in dragging the arms inward.

subject: physics
question_text: A solid disc and a ring of the same mass and radius are released together from the top of the same incline and roll without slipping. Which reaches the bottom first, and why?
_chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
_concept: rolling motion and moment of inertia
_answer: The disc wins — its moment of inertia (½MR²) is smaller than the ring's (MR²), so less of its energy goes into rotation and it gains more translational speed.
_explanation: For rolling bodies, gravitational potential energy splits between translational and rotational kinetic energy in a ratio set by I/MR². The ring stores a larger fraction in rotation, leaving less for forward motion, so the disc accelerates faster and arrives first — independent of their masses and radii.

subject: physics
question_text: Is it possible for the centre of mass of an object to lie at a point where there is no matter at all? Support your answer with an example.
_chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
_concept: centre of mass can lie outside the body
_answer: Yes — for a uniform ring the centre of mass is at the empty geometric centre; an L-shaped lamina or a boomerang also has its centre of mass outside the material.
_explanation: The centre of mass is a mathematical average of mass positions, not a physical particle. For symmetric hollow shapes like rings and horseshoes, the averaging places it in empty space, and the body still behaves dynamically as if all its mass were concentrated there.

subject: physics
question_text: Can a set of forces on a rigid body produce zero net force but a nonzero net torque? What everyday action demonstrates this?
_chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
_concept: couple: zero net force with net torque
_answer: Yes — a couple (two equal, opposite, parallel forces along different lines) has zero net force but nonzero torque, e.g., the two hands turning a steering wheel or fingers opening a bottle cap.
_explanation: Net force determines translation while torque determines rotation, and they are independent. Two equal and opposite forces applied at different points cancel as forces but their moments add, producing pure rotation without any acceleration of the centre of mass.

subject: physics
question_text: Astronauts float 'weightlessly' inside the International Space Station, about 400 km above Earth. Is gravity actually negligible at that altitude?
_concept: weightlessness in orbit is free fall, not absence of gravity
_answer: No — gravity there is still about 90% of its surface value; astronauts float because they and the station are in continuous free fall around Earth, so there is no supporting contact force.
_explanation: Weight sensation comes from normal forces, and in orbit both astronaut and station accelerate toward Earth at the same rate, eliminating any contact force between them. Gravity is very much present — it is precisely what keeps the station curving around the planet instead of flying off in a straight line.

subject: physics
question_text: The Moon is constantly pulled toward Earth by gravity, yet it never crashes into us. In what sense is the Moon actually 'falling' all the time?
_concept: orbital motion as continuous free fall
_answer: The Moon perpetually falls toward Earth, but its large tangential velocity means it keeps missing — the fall only bends its straight-line path into a closed orbit.
_explanation: Without gravity the Moon would move in a straight line and escape; gravity continuously deflects it toward Earth. The deflection exactly matches the curvature of its orbit, so the Moon falls around Earth rather than into it — the essence of orbital motion.

subject: physics
question_text: If you could descend deep into a mine shaft toward Earth's centre, would your weight increase or decrease (treating Earth as a uniform sphere)?
_concept: variation of g below Earth's surface
_answer: It decreases — inside a uniform Earth, only the mass within your radius attracts you, so g falls linearly with depth and becomes zero at the centre.
_explanation: By the shell theorem, the spherical shell of material above you exerts zero net gravity, so the effective attracting mass shrinks as you descend. For uniform density this gives g proportional to distance from the centre, so weight steadily drops to zero at the centre.

subject: physics
question_text: Escape speed from Earth is about 11.2 km/s for a small stone and also 11.2 km/s for a massive spacecraft. Why doesn't the mass of the escaping object matter?
_concept: escape velocity is independent of projectile mass
_answer: Both the kinetic energy needed and the gravitational potential energy to overcome are proportional to the object's mass, so mass cancels: v_esc = √(2GM/R) depends only on Earth.
_explanation: Escape requires ½mv² ≥ GMm/R, and m appears on both sides of the inequality. Cancelling it shows escape speed depends only on the planet's mass and radius — though a heavier object does require proportionally more energy and fuel to reach that speed.

subject: physics
question_text: Rubber stretches enormously and steel barely stretches at all, yet physicists call steel more 'elastic' than rubber. What definition of elasticity makes this true?
_concept: elasticity measured by Young's modulus, not stretchability
_answer: Elasticity measures resistance to deformation and fidelity of recovery — steel has a far larger Young's modulus, deforming much less under the same stress and returning precisely to shape.
_explanation: In physics, a more elastic material is one requiring greater stress to produce a given strain, quantified by Young's modulus. Steel's modulus is vastly higher than rubber's, so steel is the more elastic material even though rubber is more stretchable.

subject: physics
question_text: For the same mass of material, engineers prefer a hollow tube over a solid rod as a shaft or beam. Why does moving material away from the axis make the structure stronger against bending and twisting?
_concept: hollow shafts resist torsion/bending better per unit mass
_answer: Material far from the axis experiences larger strain and contributes disproportionately to restoring torque, so distributing the same mass at a larger radius greatly increases stiffness against twisting and bending.
_explanation: In bending or torsion, layers near the axis are barely strained and contribute little resistance. Placing the material at a larger radius lets every bit of it work near maximum strain, which is why a hollow tube of the same mass is stiffer than a solid rod — and why bones and bamboo are hollow.

subject: physics
question_text: Stress has units of pressure, but the strain it produces is a pure number with no units at all. Why does strain have no units?
_answer: Strain is the ratio of change in dimension to original dimension (e.g., ΔL/L), so the units cancel, leaving a dimensionless number.
_explanation: Strain quantifies fractional deformation — how much an object changed relative to its own size. Being a ratio of two like quantities, it is dimensionless, which lets Young's modulus (stress/strain) carry the same units as stress.

subject: physics
question_text: An ice cube floats in a glass filled to the brim with water. When the ice melts completely, does the glass overflow, does the level drop, or does it stay exactly at the brim?
_answer: The level stays exactly the same — floating ice displaces water equal to its weight, and on melting it turns into precisely that volume of water.
_explanation: By Archimedes' principle, the floating cube displaces a water volume whose weight equals the cube's weight. When the ice melts, its mass becomes water that occupies exactly the volume it was displacing, so the level neither rises nor falls.

subject: physics
question_text: A hydraulic lift lets a person pressing a small piston raise a car on a large piston. Force is multiplied many times — is energy multiplied too?
_concept: Pascal's law multiplies force, not energy
_answer: No — the small piston must move a proportionally larger distance than the large piston, so work (force × distance) is conserved; only force is amplified.
_explanation: Pascal's law transmits pressure equally, so the large piston feels a bigger force in proportion to its area. But the incompressible fluid volume shifted is the same on both sides, making the large piston's displacement smaller by the same ratio — energy in equals energy out (minus losses).

subject: physics
question_text: A spinning cricket ball curves sideways through the air even though gravity only acts downward. What creates the sideways force?
_answer: The spin drags air around the ball, making air move faster on one side and slower on the other; by Bernoulli's principle the fast side has lower pressure, producing a net sideways force (Magnus effect).
_explanation: A spinning ball's surface carries air with it, adding to the airstream speed on one side and subtracting on the other. The resulting pressure difference — lower pressure where flow is faster — pushes the ball toward the low-pressure side, curving its trajectory.

subject: physics
question_text: Water climbs upward inside a narrow glass capillary tube, but mercury in the same tube is pushed down below the outside level. What property difference explains the opposite behaviours?
_answer: Water wets glass (adhesion beats cohesion, contact angle < 90°) so its concave meniscus pulls it up; mercury doesn't wet glass (cohesion dominates, contact angle > 90°) so its convex meniscus depresses it.
_explanation: Capillary action depends on the balance between adhesion to the wall and cohesion within the liquid, summarized by the contact angle. An acute contact angle gives a concave meniscus whose surface-tension pull raises the liquid; an obtuse angle, as with mercury on glass, gives a convex meniscus and depression.

subject: physics
question_text: On a hot day, water stored in an unglazed earthen pot stays noticeably cooler than water in a metal or plastic container. What physics keeps the pot's water cool?
_answer: Water seeps through the pot's pores and evaporates from the surface, and the large latent heat of vaporization is drawn from the remaining water, cooling it.
_explanation: Evaporation requires latent heat, which the escaping molecules take from the water left behind. The porous clay maintains a constantly wet outer surface for continuous evaporation, so the pot works as a natural evaporative cooler — most effective in hot, dry air.

subject: physics
question_text: A metal plate has a circular hole in the middle. When the plate is heated uniformly, does the hole become larger, smaller, or stay the same size?
_answer: Larger — every linear dimension of the plate expands, so the hole expands as if it were made of the same metal (like a photographic enlargement).
_explanation: Uniform heating scales up all distances between atoms by the same fraction, so the whole plate, including the hole's boundary, expands proportionally. The material does not creep inward to fill the hole; this is why a heated metal ring slips more easily onto a shaft.

subject: physics
question_text: To chill a drink you can add 100 g of ice at 0°C or 100 g of liquid water at 0°C. Both are at the same temperature — why is the ice dramatically more effective?
_answer: Melting the ice absorbs its latent heat of fusion (about 334 J per gram) from the drink before any warming happens, whereas 0°C water can only absorb heat by warming up.
_explanation: Temperature alone doesn't measure how much heat something can soak up. Ice must first absorb a large latent heat just to become water at the same 0°C, and only then does it warm like ordinary water — so gram for gram, ice extracts far more heat from the drink.

subject: physics
question_text: On a hot day, someone suggests cooling the kitchen by leaving the refrigerator door wide open. Will this cool the room, and what does thermodynamics say happens instead?
_concept: refrigerator as a heat pump; energy balance
_answer: No — the room actually warms up: the fridge dumps all the heat it extracts plus the electrical work it consumes back into the same room through its rear coils.
_explanation: A refrigerator doesn't destroy heat; it moves heat from inside to its condenser coils, adding the compressor's work on top. With the door open, the heat removed from the room air is returned to the room plus extra work input, so the net effect is heating.

subject: physics
question_text: To raise the temperature of a gas by 1°C, you need more heat at constant pressure than at constant volume (Cp > Cv). Where does the extra heat go?
_answer: At constant pressure the gas expands and does work on the surroundings, so heat must supply that expansion work in addition to raising internal energy; at constant volume no work is done.
_explanation: The first law says heat input goes into internal energy plus work done by the gas. At constant volume all heat raises temperature, but at constant pressure part of the heat is spent pushing back the surroundings as the gas expands, making Cp larger than Cv by R for an ideal gas.

subject: physics
question_text: An ideal gas in an insulated container suddenly expands into an adjacent vacuum. No heat enters and, surprisingly, its temperature does not change. Why not?
_concept: free expansion of an ideal gas
_answer: In free expansion the gas pushes against nothing, so it does zero work; with no heat exchange either, internal energy — which for an ideal gas depends only on temperature — is unchanged.
_explanation: Work requires pushing against an opposing pressure, and a vacuum offers none, so W = 0; the insulation ensures Q = 0, hence ΔU = 0. Since an ideal gas's internal energy is purely a function of temperature, the temperature stays constant even though volume and pressure change.

subject: physics
question_text: Even a perfect, frictionless heat engine cannot convert all the heat it absorbs into work. What fundamental principle forbids 100% efficiency?
_concept: second law of thermodynamics and Carnot limit
_answer: The second law of thermodynamics — a cyclic engine must reject some heat to a colder reservoir, capping efficiency at the Carnot value 1 − Tc/Th, which is below 100% unless the sink is at absolute zero.
_explanation: The Kelvin-Planck statement forbids any cyclic device whose sole effect is converting heat entirely into work. Some heat must always flow to a cold sink to complete the cycle, so even an ideal reversible engine's efficiency is limited by the reservoir temperatures.

subject: physics
question_text: A container holds a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gas at the same temperature. Which molecules have greater average translational kinetic energy, and which move faster on average?
_concept: equipartition: average KE depends only on temperature
_answer: Their average translational kinetic energies are equal (each is (3/2)kT), but the lighter hydrogen molecules move about four times faster since v_rms ∝ 1/√M.
_explanation: Temperature fixes average translational kinetic energy per molecule regardless of the gas's identity. Equal ½mv² with a 16-times smaller mass means hydrogen's rms speed is √16 = 4 times oxygen's.

subject: physics
question_text: A sealed rigid container of gas is heated. Nothing is added and the volume can't change, yet the pressure rises. Explain the pressure increase in terms of molecular motion.
_answer: Heating raises molecular speeds, so molecules hit the walls both harder (greater momentum transfer per collision) and more often, increasing the average force per unit area.
_explanation: Gas pressure is the cumulative effect of molecular impacts on the walls. Higher temperature means higher rms speed, which increases the momentum change in each wall collision and the collision frequency, and both effects together raise the pressure.

subject: physics
question_text: Heating one mole of nitrogen by 1 K takes more energy than heating one mole of helium by 1 K, even at the same conditions. What do nitrogen molecules do with the extra energy?
_concept: degrees of freedom and molar heat capacity
_answer: Diatomic nitrogen also stores energy in two rotational degrees of freedom, so by equipartition it needs (5/2)R per kelvin versus helium's (3/2)R for translation alone.
_explanation: Equipartition assigns ½kT per molecule to each accessible degree of freedom. Monatomic helium has only 3 translational modes, while diatomic nitrogen adds 2 rotational modes at ordinary temperatures, so more heat is needed to achieve the same temperature rise.

subject: physics
question_text: A simple pendulum is set oscillating inside a lift. The lift's cable snaps and it falls freely. What happens to the pendulum's time period during the fall?
_concept: pendulum in free fall — effective gravity
_answer: The period becomes infinite — effective gravity inside the falling lift is zero, so there is no restoring torque and the pendulum stops oscillating.
_explanation: A pendulum's restoring force comes from gravity, with T = 2π√(L/g_eff). In free fall the effective g is zero, so a displaced bob feels no pull back toward the mean position; it simply stays where it is (or circles with any speed it had) instead of oscillating.

subject: physics
question_text: A block oscillating on a spring is pulled to double its previous amplitude and released. It now travels a longer path each cycle — does its time period increase?
_concept: period of SHM is independent of amplitude
_answer: No — the period stays exactly the same: larger amplitude means proportionally larger restoring forces and speeds, and T = 2π√(m/k) contains no amplitude.
_explanation: In simple harmonic motion the restoring force grows linearly with displacement, so a farther-travelling block also moves faster in just the right proportion. The longer path and the higher average speed cancel, making the period independent of amplitude — the defining feature of SHM.

subject: physics
question_text: For a particle in simple harmonic motion, at which point is its speed maximum, and at which point is its acceleration maximum? Why are these two points different?
_concept: phase relation of velocity and acceleration in SHM
_answer: Speed is maximum at the mean position (where acceleration is zero); acceleration is maximum at the extreme positions (where speed is zero), because acceleration is proportional to displacement.
_explanation: The restoring force, and hence acceleration, is proportional to displacement from the mean, peaking at the extremes and vanishing at the centre. Energy considerations mirror this: all energy is kinetic at the mean position and all potential at the extremes.

subject: physics
question_text: Soldiers marching in perfect step are ordered to break step while crossing a suspension bridge. What danger is this precaution guarding against?
_answer: Resonance — if the rhythmic footfalls match the bridge's natural frequency, oscillation amplitude can grow dangerously large; random steps prevent coherent periodic forcing.
_explanation: A periodic driving force near a structure's natural frequency pumps energy into the oscillation every cycle, letting the amplitude build up enormously. Breaking step randomizes the force's timing so no single frequency dominates and resonance cannot develop.

subject: physics
question_text: You can clearly hear a person talking from around the corner of a building, but you cannot see them. Both sound and light are waves — why does sound bend around the corner while light doesn't (noticeably)?
_concept: diffraction depends on wavelength vs obstacle size
_answer: Diffraction is significant only when the wavelength is comparable to the obstacle; audible sound has wavelengths of centimetres to metres, matching buildings, while light's wavelength (~half a micron) is far too small.
_explanation: All waves diffract, but the bending is appreciable only when the obstacle or opening is of the same order as the wavelength. Sound's metre-scale wavelengths spread easily around everyday objects, whereas visible light's sub-micron wavelengths make its bending around a wall utterly negligible.

subject: physics
question_text: Does sound travel faster or slower through humid air than through dry air at the same temperature and pressure? The answer surprises most people — justify it.
_concept: speed of sound and density of the medium
_answer: Faster in humid air — water vapour (molar mass 18) is lighter than the nitrogen/oxygen it displaces (average ~29), lowering the air's density, and v = √(γP/ρ) rises as density falls.
_explanation: People assume humid air is 'heavier', but adding water vapour actually lowers the average molar mass and density of air at fixed pressure. Since sound speed varies inversely with the square root of density, sound travels slightly faster on humid days.

subject: physics
question_text: Two tuning forks of nearly equal frequency are sounded together, and the loudness rises and falls rhythmically. Neither fork's loudness is changing — what causes the throbbing?
_concept: beats from superposition of close frequencies
_answer: Beats — the two waves drift in and out of phase, alternately interfering constructively (loud) and destructively (soft), with beat frequency equal to the difference of the two frequencies.
_explanation: Superposing two waves of slightly different frequencies produces a resultant whose amplitude slowly oscillates as the relative phase cycles from aligned to opposed. The ear hears this amplitude envelope as periodic waxing and waning of loudness at the difference frequency.

subject: physics
question_text: As an ambulance speeds past you, its siren's pitch audibly drops. Has the speed of the sound waves in the air changed as the ambulance moves?
_concept: Doppler effect changes frequency, not wave speed
_answer: No — sound speed is fixed by the air itself; the moving source compresses wavefronts ahead and stretches them behind, changing the wavelength and hence the frequency you receive.
_explanation: Once emitted, sound travels at a speed determined by the medium, independent of the source's motion. A source moving toward you crowds successive wavefronts closer together (shorter wavelength, higher pitch) and spaces them out behind (lower pitch) — that switch is what you hear as it passes.

subject: physics
question_text: In a standing wave on a stretched string, certain points never move at all, no matter how violently the rest of the string vibrates. How can parts of a vibrating string remain permanently still?
_answer: At nodes, the two oppositely travelling waves that form the standing wave always arrive exactly out of phase, so their displacements cancel at every instant.
_explanation: A standing wave is the superposition of identical waves travelling in opposite directions. At specific points spaced half a wavelength apart, the crest of one wave always coincides with the trough of the other, giving permanent destructive interference — the nodes — while midway points (antinodes) oscillate maximally.

subject: physics
question_text: A plastic comb rubbed through dry hair picks up tiny bits of paper even though the paper is electrically neutral. How can a charged object attract something with zero net charge?
_concept: attraction of neutral objects by induction/polarization
_answer: The comb's field polarizes the paper, pulling opposite charges slightly nearer and like charges farther; since the field is stronger closer to the comb, attraction on the near charges wins.
_explanation: A charged body induces charge separation in a neutral object: unlike charges shift toward it and like charges away. Because electric force weakens with distance, the nearer (unlike) charges feel a stronger pull than the farther (like) charges feel a push, giving a net attraction.

subject: physics
question_text: In electrostatic conditions, the electric field everywhere inside the material of a conductor is exactly zero — no matter how strongly the conductor is charged. What makes this happen automatically?
_concept: field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium
_answer: Free electrons move in response to any internal field and redistribute on the surface until the field they create exactly cancels the applied field inside; motion stops only when the interior field is zero.
_explanation: A conductor contains mobile charges, so any nonzero internal field would drive currents, contradicting the assumption of electrostatics. The charges therefore rearrange themselves — all excess charge sitting on the surface — until their field precisely cancels any external field within the material.

subject: physics
question_text: Why can two electric field lines never intersect each other at a point in space?
_answer: The tangent to a field line gives the direction of the electric field; intersecting lines would assign two different directions to the field at one point, which is impossible since the field is unique there.
_explanation: At any point, the net electric field is a single, well-defined vector. If two field lines crossed, their two tangents at the crossing would imply two simultaneous field directions at that point — a contradiction, so field lines must never intersect.

subject: physics
question_text: A closed surface contains no charge inside it, but a large charge sits just outside the surface. The field on the surface is clearly nonzero — yet the total electric flux through the surface is zero. Reconcile these facts.
_concept: Gauss's law: flux depends only on enclosed charge
_answer: Every field line from the outside charge that enters the surface also exits it, so incoming (negative) and outgoing (positive) flux cancel exactly; Gauss's law counts only enclosed charge.
_explanation: Flux measures the net number of field lines crossing outward. An external charge's lines pierce the closed surface an even number of times — in and back out — contributing zero net flux, which is why Gauss's law equates total flux solely to charge enclosed divided by ε₀.

subject: physics
question_text: Exactly midway between two equal positive charges, the electric field is zero. Is the electric potential at that point also zero?
_concept: field can vanish where potential does not
_answer: No — the potential there is positive and equals twice the potential due to either charge; field is a vector that cancels, but potential is a scalar that adds.
_explanation: The two charges produce oppositely directed fields at the midpoint, which cancel as vectors. Potentials, however, are scalars with no direction: each charge contributes a positive kq/r, and they simply add — showing zero field does not imply zero potential.

subject: physics
question_text: During a lightning storm, a car is considered one of the safest places to be. It's popularly credited to the rubber tyres — what is the real reason?
_answer: The metal body acts as a Faraday cage — charge and current stay on the outer conducting shell and the field inside a conductor's cavity is essentially zero; a few centimetres of rubber is irrelevant against millions of volts.
_explanation: A conducting enclosure shields its interior: induced charges arrange on the outer surface so the field inside the cavity vanishes, and lightning current flows around the shell to ground. Rubber tyres offer no meaningful insulation to a discharge that has already jumped kilometres of air.

subject: physics
question_text: A charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery, and then a dielectric slab is slipped between its plates. The stored energy decreases. The charge hasn't changed — where did the missing energy go?
_concept: energy change on inserting a dielectric at constant charge
_answer: The fringing field pulls the slab inward, so the capacitor does positive work on the slab as it enters; that work accounts for the drop in stored energy U = Q²/2C as C increases.
_explanation: With charge fixed, energy is Q²/2C, and inserting a dielectric raises C, lowering U. The energy isn't lost: the non-uniform edge field exerts an attractive force that draws the slab in, transferring energy to the slab (as kinetic energy, or as work against whoever inserts it slowly).

subject: physics
question_text: Doubling the charge placed on a capacitor also doubles the voltage across it, so the ratio Q/V never changes. Why is capacitance a property only of geometry and the dielectric, not of how much charge is stored?
_answer: Field and potential are directly proportional to charge (superposition), so V always scales linearly with Q; the constant ratio C = Q/V is set by plate size, separation, and dielectric alone.
_explanation: Electrostatics is linear: doubling all charges doubles the field everywhere and hence doubles the potential difference. The proportionality constant between Q and V therefore depends only on the arrangement of the conductors and the medium between them — which is what capacitance measures.

subject: physics
question_text: Electrons drift through a wire at less than a millimetre per second, yet a bulb lights up the instant you flip a switch across the room. How?
_concept: drift velocity vs signal propagation speed
_answer: The electric field is established through the circuit at nearly the speed of light, setting electrons everywhere in the wire — including inside the bulb — drifting almost simultaneously; you don't wait for electrons from the switch to arrive.
_explanation: A wire is already full of free electrons, like a pipe full of water. Closing the switch propagates the electric field through the circuit almost instantly, and that field pushes on all the electrons at once, so current begins everywhere in the loop essentially immediately despite the tiny drift speed.

subject: physics
question_text: Heating a copper wire increases its resistance, but heating a piece of pure silicon decreases its resistance. What opposite mechanisms are at play?
_concept: temperature dependence of resistivity in metals vs semiconductors
_answer: In copper the carrier count is fixed, and hotter lattice vibrations scatter electrons more, raising resistance; in silicon heating frees exponentially more electron-hole pairs, and the surge in carriers overwhelms the extra scattering.
_explanation: A metal's conduction electron density barely changes with temperature, so increased lattice vibration and scattering dominate, reducing relaxation time. In a semiconductor, thermal energy promotes many more electrons across the band gap, and this rapid growth in carrier number drives resistivity down.

subject: physics
question_text: A battery is labelled 12 V, but while it drives a large current through a circuit, a voltmeter across its terminals reads noticeably less than 12 V. Where do the missing volts go?
_concept: emf, internal resistance and terminal voltage
_answer: Across the battery's own internal resistance — terminal voltage V = emf − I·r, so the larger the current, the more potential drops inside the battery itself.
_explanation: A real battery behaves like an ideal emf in series with a small internal resistance r. When current flows, I·r of potential is 'used up' inside the battery, so the terminals deliver less than the full emf — and the reading approaches 12 V only when the current drawn is tiny.

subject: physics
question_text: A metal wire is uniformly stretched to twice its original length without changing its volume. By what factor does its resistance change, and why is it more than double?
_answer: Resistance becomes 4 times: length doubles and, with volume constant, cross-sectional area halves, and R = ρL/A gets hit by both changes (2 × 2 = 4).
_explanation: Stretching affects resistance twice over — electrons must travel a longer path, and they travel it through a thinner cross-section. With volume fixed, doubling L halves A, so R = ρL/A grows by a factor of four, not two.

subject: physics
question_text: A charged particle moves through a strong magnetic field, which continuously exerts force on it. Yet the magnetic force can never change the particle's speed or kinetic energy. Why not?
_answer: The magnetic force F = qv×B is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does zero work; it can only bend the path, changing direction but never speed.
_explanation: Work requires a force component along the motion, and the cross product v×B guarantees the magnetic force is perpendicular to v at every instant. The force therefore acts as a perfect steering agent — curving the trajectory into circles or helices — without ever adding or removing kinetic energy.

subject: physics
question_text: A proton is fired into a uniform magnetic field with its velocity exactly parallel to the field lines. Describe its subsequent path.
_concept: motion of a charge parallel to a magnetic field
_answer: It continues in a straight line at constant speed — the magnetic force qv×B is zero when v is parallel (or antiparallel) to B.
_explanation: The magnitude of the magnetic force is qvB·sinθ, and sinθ = 0 for parallel motion, so the field exerts no force at all. With no force, Newton's first law takes over and the proton moves undeviated along the field direction.

subject: physics
question_text: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. Do they attract or repel each other, and through what mechanism does one wire 'feel' the other?
_answer: They attract — each wire sits in the circular magnetic field of the other, and the force F = IL×B on each points toward its neighbour; antiparallel currents would repel.
_explanation: A current creates a magnetic field circling it, and a second current-carrying wire placed in that field experiences a force. Applying the right-hand rules shows the force is attractive for like-directed currents — the effect historically used to define the ampere.

subject: physics
question_text: Hoping to separate a north pole from a south pole, you cut a bar magnet exactly in half between its poles. What do you actually get, and what does this reveal about magnetism?
_answer: Two complete, smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole — isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist because magnetism arises from atomic current loops, which are always dipoles.
_explanation: A magnet's field originates in circulating and spinning electrons, each acting as a tiny dipole; poles are just the faces where these aligned dipoles' effects emerge. Cutting the magnet merely exposes new faces, so every fragment, down to the atomic scale, remains a dipole.

subject: physics
question_text: A strong permanent magnet is heated in a flame until red hot and then loses virtually all its magnetism. What happened inside it?
_concept: Curie temperature and loss of ferromagnetism
_answer: Above its Curie temperature, thermal agitation randomizes the aligned atomic dipoles/domains, destroying the spontaneous order — the ferromagnet becomes a paramagnet.
_explanation: Ferromagnetism relies on atomic magnetic moments locking into aligned domains. Heating supplies random thermal energy that eventually overwhelms this alignment; beyond the Curie point the ordered domains disintegrate and the material retains no permanent magnetization.

subject: physics
question_text: Electric field lines start on positive charges and end on negative ones, but magnetic field lines never begin or end anywhere — they always form closed loops. What deep fact about magnetism does this reflect?
_concept: closed magnetic field lines and absence of monopoles
_answer: There are no magnetic monopoles — no isolated 'magnetic charges' to act as sources or sinks — so lines must close on themselves, and the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero (Gauss's law for magnetism).
_explanation: Field lines can terminate only on the corresponding 'charge', and no magnetic analogue of electric charge has ever been found. Consequently every magnetic field line that leaves a magnet's north pole loops around and re-enters at the south pole, continuing through the magnet's interior.

subject: physics
question_text: A strong magnet dropped through a vertical copper pipe falls eerily slowly, even though copper is not magnetic. What slows it down?
_answer: The falling magnet's changing flux induces eddy currents in the pipe, and by Lenz's law these currents create magnetic fields that oppose the magnet's motion, producing a retarding force.
_explanation: As the magnet moves, the magnetic flux through each section of the conducting pipe changes, inducing circulating eddy currents. Lenz's law guarantees these currents flow so as to oppose the change causing them — effectively braking the magnet, which drifts down at a slow terminal speed.

subject: physics
question_text: Lenz's law insists that an induced current must always oppose the change that produces it. What catastrophic violation of physics would occur if the induced current instead aided the change?
_concept: Lenz's law as a consequence of energy conservation
_answer: Energy conservation would be violated — an aiding current would strengthen the change, inducing more current, giving runaway motion and free energy from nothing (a perpetual motion machine).
_explanation: If pushing a magnet toward a coil induced a current that pulled the magnet in faster, the flux change would grow, inducing still more current, and kinetic plus electrical energy would multiply without any input. Opposition ensures you must do work against the induced effects to generate electrical energy.

subject: physics
question_text: Can an emf be induced in a coil that is held completely stationary, with no part of the circuit moving at all? If so, how?
_concept: induction by time-varying magnetic flux without motion
_answer: Yes — any change of magnetic flux through the coil induces an emf, so a time-varying magnetic field (e.g., from a nearby AC electromagnet or a moving magnet) induces emf in a stationary coil.
_explanation: Faraday's law depends on the rate of change of flux, not on motion of the conductor. Flux can change because the field itself varies with time, which is exactly how transformers work: a changing current in one stationary coil induces emf in another stationary coil.

subject: physics
question_text: A transformer effortlessly steps AC voltages up or down, but connect it to a steady DC supply and the output is zero (and the coil may even burn out). Why does a transformer fundamentally need AC?
_answer: Induction requires changing magnetic flux; steady DC creates a constant flux, so no emf is induced in the secondary — and without back-emf, the primary draws a dangerously large current.
_explanation: A transformer transfers energy via Faraday induction: the alternating primary current creates an oscillating flux in the core, which induces emf in the secondary. DC produces constant flux and hence zero induced emf, while the absence of opposing back-emf leaves only the primary's small resistance to limit current, overheating it.

subject: physics
question_text: An AC source connected to a capacitor drives a steady alternating current in the circuit, yet no charge ever actually crosses the insulating gap between the plates. How can current 'flow' in such a circuit?
_answer: The AC source repeatedly charges and discharges the plates, so charge continually surges back and forth in the connecting wires — a genuine circuit current — even though no charge crosses the dielectric gap.
_explanation: Each half-cycle, electrons pile onto one plate and drain from the other, then reverse. This oscillating charging current in the wires is what the ammeter reads; the capacitor passes AC in this effective sense while completely blocking steady DC once fully charged.

subject: physics
question_text: In a series LCR circuit near resonance, a voltmeter can read a larger voltage across the inductor alone than the source supplies to the whole circuit. How is this possible without violating any law?
_concept: phasor addition and voltage magnification at resonance
_answer: The inductor and capacitor voltages are 180° out of phase and largely cancel each other; individually each can far exceed the source voltage, while their phasor sum with the resistor's voltage still equals the source voltage.
_explanation: AC voltages add as phasors, not arithmetically. Near resonance, V_L and V_C are huge but opposite in phase, so they nearly cancel, leaving the modest source voltage across the resistor — energy sloshes back and forth between L and C, building large individual voltages.

subject: physics
question_text: Sound cannot cross the vacuum of space, yet sunlight crosses 150 million kilometres of vacuum to reach Earth. If waves need something to 'wave', what is oscillating in light travelling through empty space?
_concept: EM waves are self-sustaining field oscillations
_answer: Oscillating electric and magnetic fields — a changing E field generates a changing B field and vice versa, so the wave sustains itself and needs no material medium.
_explanation: Mechanical waves like sound are disturbances of matter, but electromagnetic waves are travelling oscillations of the E and B fields themselves. Maxwell showed each changing field regenerates the other, letting the pair propagate through vacuum at speed c with the fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel.

subject: physics
question_text: A microwave oven heats a bowl of soup quickly, while the ceramic bowl itself stays comparatively cool. Why do microwaves selectively heat the food?
_answer: Water molecules are polar; the oscillating microwave field makes these dipoles flip back and forth rapidly, and this agitation spreads as heat — dry, non-polar ceramic absorbs far less.
_explanation: Microwaves couple strongly to permanent electric dipoles like water. The alternating field torques the molecules millions of times per second, and intermolecular friction converts that rotational jiggling into thermal energy, so water-rich food heats fast while dry containers lag behind.

subject: physics
question_text: A swimming pool always looks shallower than it really is when viewed from above. What bends the light to create this illusion?
_answer: Refraction — light from the bottom bends away from the normal on leaving water for air, so the rays appear to come from a raised point; apparent depth ≈ real depth divided by the refractive index (~3/4 of real depth).
_explanation: Rays leaving a denser medium bend away from the normal at the surface. Your eye traces the refracted rays backward along straight lines, locating the image of the pool floor above its true position — which is why pools are deceptively deep.

subject: physics
question_text: A diamond and a piece of glass can be cut into identical shapes, yet the diamond sparkles far more brilliantly. What optical property of diamond is chiefly responsible?
_concept: total internal reflection and critical angle in diamond
_answer: Diamond's very high refractive index (~2.42) gives it a tiny critical angle (~24.4°), so light entering it undergoes repeated total internal reflection before exiting, concentrated into brilliant flashes.
_explanation: The critical angle shrinks as refractive index rises, so inside diamond most internal rays strike facets beyond the critical angle and are totally reflected instead of leaking out. Skilled cutting exploits this to trap light through multiple bounces, releasing it through the top in intense sparkles.

subject: physics
question_text: A plane mirror forms a virtual image — light rays never actually pass through the image location. Can a camera nevertheless photograph your image in a mirror? Explain.
_answer: Yes — the reflected rays really exist and diverge as if from the virtual image; the camera's lens converges those rays into a real image on its sensor, exactly as your eye's lens does.
_explanation: 'Virtual' only means the rays don't physically pass through the image point, not that the light is fake. A camera intercepts the genuinely diverging reflected rays and refracts them to a real focus on the sensor — which is precisely how your eye sees the mirror image too.

subject: physics
question_text: A mirror seems to swap your left and right hands, but it never swaps your head and feet. Why would a mirror treat the horizontal direction differently from the vertical?
_concept: mirror inversion is front-back, not left-right
_answer: It doesn't — a plane mirror actually inverts front and back (the direction perpendicular to its surface); the 'left-right swap' is our interpretation from mentally rotating ourselves about a vertical axis to face the image.
_explanation: The mirror maps every point straight through to an equal distance behind the glass, reversing only the axis perpendicular to the mirror. When we imagine stepping into our image, we picture turning about a vertical axis, and it is that imagined rotation — not the mirror — that exchanges left and right while leaving up and down alone.

subject: physics
question_text: Light from two separate torch bulbs shining on the same wall never produces interference fringes, yet light from two pinholes lit by a single bulb can. What crucial ingredient do the two independent bulbs lack?
_answer: Coherence — independent sources emit with randomly and rapidly changing relative phase, so the interference pattern shifts billions of times per second and averages to uniform illumination; a sustained pattern needs a constant phase difference.
_explanation: Interference fringes are stable only if the phase difference between the two waves stays fixed. Atoms in separate bulbs emit uncorrelated wavetrains whose relative phase jumps randomly, washing out any pattern; deriving both beams from one source locks their phases together.

subject: physics
question_text: In Young's double-slit experiment, the dark fringes are places where light plus light gives darkness. Is light energy being destroyed at these dark fringes?
_answer: No — energy is redistributed, not destroyed: the bright fringes receive more than the sum of the two beams' average intensity (4I₀ instead of 2I₀), exactly compensating for the darkness elsewhere.
_explanation: Interference rearranges where energy lands on the screen without changing the total. Averaged over the pattern, the intensity equals the sum from both slits; the deficit at destructive-fringe locations is precisely balanced by the excess at constructive ones.

subject: physics
question_text: Polaroid sunglasses are far better at cutting glare from a lake's surface than ordinary tinted glasses of the same darkness. What is special about reflected glare that Polaroids exploit?
_answer: Light reflected off horizontal surfaces is partially (at Brewster's angle, completely) polarized horizontally; Polaroid lenses with a vertical transmission axis selectively block this polarized glare while passing much other light.
_explanation: Reflection from non-metallic surfaces favours the polarization component parallel to the surface, so glare is predominantly horizontally polarized. A vertically oriented polaroid absorbs this component almost entirely — killing glare specifically — whereas plain tinting dims everything equally.

subject: physics
question_text: Shine red light of enormous intensity on a metal and no photoelectrons emerge, yet even feeble violet light ejects them instantly. Why can't sheer intensity make up for low frequency?
_chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
_concept: photoelectric effect: photon energy depends on frequency
_answer: Emission is a one-photon-one-electron process: each photon carries energy hf, and if hf is below the work function, no single photon can free an electron — intensity only increases the number of (individually inadequate) photons.
_explanation: An electron absorbs light one photon at a time and needs at least the work function's worth of energy in that single event. Below the threshold frequency every photon falls short regardless of how many arrive, while above it even a dim beam ejects electrons immediately — the observation that shattered the classical wave picture.

subject: physics
question_text: In a photoelectric experiment, making the light brighter increases the photocurrent but leaves the stopping potential completely unchanged. What does this tell us about what intensity does and doesn't control?
_chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
_concept: intensity vs frequency roles in photoelectric emission
_answer: Intensity controls only the number of photons, hence the number of ejected electrons (current); the maximum kinetic energy per electron — and thus the stopping potential — is fixed by photon energy hf minus the work function.
_explanation: Each photoelectron gets its energy from one photon, so its maximum kinetic energy depends solely on the light's frequency and the metal's work function. Brighter light of the same colour just means more photons ejecting more electrons, raising current without changing any individual electron's energy.

subject: physics
question_text: Electrons show diffraction patterns just like waves, and de Broglie says every moving object has a wavelength. Why does a bowled cricket ball never show any wave-like behaviour?
_chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
_concept: de Broglie wavelength of macroscopic objects
_answer: Its de Broglie wavelength λ = h/mv is fantastically small (~10⁻³⁴ m for a cricket ball) — dozens of orders of magnitude below any obstacle or slit — so diffraction effects are utterly unobservable.
_explanation: Wave effects appear only when the wavelength is comparable to the structures light or matter interacts with. Planck's constant is so tiny that macroscopic momenta give wavelengths far smaller than an atomic nucleus, which is why quantum wave behaviour is only detectable for particles like electrons.

subject: physics
question_text: According to classical electromagnetism, an electron circling a nucleus is accelerating and must radiate energy, spiralling into the nucleus within nanoseconds. How did Bohr's model rescue the atom from this collapse?
_concept: Bohr's stationary orbits resolve classical instability
_answer: Bohr postulated that electrons in certain quantized orbits (angular momentum = nh/2π) are in 'stationary states' that simply do not radiate; energy is emitted only in discrete jumps between such orbits.
_explanation: Bohr broke with classical physics by decree: in his allowed orbits, the usual rule that accelerating charges radiate is suspended. Radiation occurs only during transitions between levels, with photon energy equal to the energy difference — an ad hoc fix later justified by full quantum mechanics.

subject: physics
question_text: When hydrogen gas is excited, it emits light only at certain sharp, specific wavelengths rather than a continuous rainbow. What does this line spectrum reveal about the atom's internal structure?
_concept: discrete spectra imply quantized energy levels
_answer: The atom's energy levels are quantized — electrons can occupy only discrete energies, so emitted photons carry only the specific energy differences between levels, producing sharp lines.
_explanation: If electrons could hold any energy, transitions would produce a continuous spectrum. The observed discrete lines mean only particular energy states exist, and each spectral line corresponds to a jump between two of them with photon energy hf = E_upper − E_lower — direct fingerprint evidence of quantization.

subject: physics
question_text: In Rutherford's experiment, almost all alpha particles sailed straight through gold foil, but about 1 in 8000 bounced back at large angles. Why did this rare backscattering demolish the 'plum pudding' model of the atom?
_concept: alpha scattering and the nuclear model
_answer: Backscattering requires an encounter with an extremely dense, concentrated positive charge; the smeared-out charge of the plum pudding model could deflect alphas only slightly, so the atom's positive charge and mass must be packed into a tiny nucleus.
_explanation: A diffuse positive sphere produces only weak fields and tiny deflections. Head-on reversal of a fast alpha particle demands an enormous repulsive force, possible only if nearly all the atom's positive charge and mass sit within a region ~10⁻¹⁴ m across — while the near-total transparency showed atoms are mostly empty space.

subject: physics
question_text: Fusing light nuclei like hydrogen releases energy, and splitting heavy nuclei like uranium also releases energy. How can both joining and breaking nuclei be energy-releasing without contradiction?
_answer: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron (A ≈ 56); any reaction moving nucleons toward that peak — fusion from the light side, fission from the heavy side — increases average binding and releases energy.
_explanation: Energy is released whenever the products are more tightly bound per nucleon than the reactants. Light nuclei climb the binding-energy curve by fusing, and very heavy nuclei climb it by splitting, so both processes head toward the same iron-region maximum from opposite directions.

subject: physics
question_text: A uranium nucleus has over 200 times the mass of a hydrogen nucleus, yet the density of nuclear matter is essentially the same in both. What does this constancy tell us about how nucleons pack?
_concept: constant nuclear density and R ∝ A^(1/3)
_answer: Nuclear radius grows as R = R₀A^(1/3), so volume is proportional to A (nucleon number); mass ∝ A and volume ∝ A give constant density (~2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³), meaning nucleons pack like incompressible spheres.
_explanation: Because volume scales directly with the number of nucleons, each nucleon occupies about the same space in every nucleus. This reflects the short-range, saturating character of the nuclear force — each nucleon binds only to its nearest neighbours, like molecules in a liquid drop.

subject: physics
question_text: Weigh a helium nucleus and you find it is measurably lighter than the combined mass of the two free protons and two free neutrons that make it up. Where did the missing mass go?
_answer: It was released as binding energy when the nucleus formed — by E = Δmc², the mass defect Δm equals the binding energy that must be supplied to pull the nucleus apart again.
_explanation: Assembling nucleons into a bound nucleus releases energy, and mass-energy equivalence means the bound system weighs less by exactly that energy divided by c². The larger the mass defect per nucleon, the more stable the nucleus — this 'missing mass' is the source of nuclear energy.

subject: physics
question_text: A p-n junction diode conducts current readily in one direction but almost none in the reverse direction. What happens at the junction to create this one-way behaviour?
_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
_answer: Forward bias lowers the depletion region's potential barrier, letting majority carriers flood across; reverse bias raises the barrier and widens the depletion region, blocking majority-carrier flow (leaving only a tiny minority-carrier current).
_explanation: Diffusion of carriers at the junction builds a depletion layer with a built-in barrier. An external voltage aligned to oppose the barrier (forward bias) shrinks it and current grows exponentially, while a reverse voltage reinforces the barrier, so the diode acts as a one-way valve.

subject: physics
question_text: At absolute zero, a piece of perfectly pure silicon would completely fail to conduct electricity — behaving like an ideal insulator. Why does an intrinsic semiconductor need heat to conduct?
_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
_concept: intrinsic carriers require thermal excitation across the band gap
_answer: At 0 K the valence band is completely full and the conduction band completely empty; with no thermal energy to excite electrons across the ~1.1 eV band gap, there are zero free carriers.
_explanation: Conduction needs mobile carriers, and in pure silicon these exist only when thermal energy promotes electrons from the valence to the conduction band, simultaneously creating holes. At absolute zero no such excitation occurs, so intrinsic silicon has literally nothing to carry current.

subject: physics
question_text: Adding just one phosphorus atom for every million silicon atoms increases silicon's conductivity thousands of times over. How can such a trace impurity have so enormous an effect?
_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
_answer: Intrinsic silicon has extremely few thermal carriers (~10¹⁶ per m³ versus ~10²⁸ atoms per m³); each pentavalent dopant donates one easily freed electron, so even one-in-a-million doping multiplies the carrier density enormously.
_explanation: Conductivity is proportional to carrier concentration, which in pure silicon is minuscule. Phosphorus's fifth valence electron is bound so weakly (~0.05 eV) that room temperature frees virtually all of them, so the donated electrons vastly outnumber the intrinsic carriers despite the tiny dopant fraction.

subject: physics
question_text: In every forward-biased diode, electrons and holes recombine and release energy — yet an LED glows visibly while an ordinary silicon diode does not. What makes the LED's recombination luminous?
_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
_concept: light emission in LEDs vs silicon diodes
_answer: LEDs use semiconductors like gallium compounds in which recombination efficiently releases energy as photons of energy roughly equal to the band gap (chosen to be in/near the visible range); in silicon, recombination energy is released predominantly as heat to the crystal lattice.
_explanation: Whether recombination produces light depends on the semiconductor's band structure and gap. LED materials are engineered so electron-hole recombination emits a photon with hf ≈ E_g, and picking the band gap tunes the colour; silicon's recombination instead dumps its energy into lattice vibrations, so it warms rather than glows.

subject: physics
question_text: Drop a feather-light pebble and a heavy boulder in vacuum and they accelerate identically. Gravity clearly pulls the boulder harder — so why doesn't it fall faster?
_concept: equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass
_answer: The gravitational force is proportional to mass, but so is inertia; in a = F/m = (GMm/r²)/m, the object's mass cancels, giving the same acceleration g for all bodies.
_explanation: A heavier object indeed feels a larger gravitational force, but it is also proportionally harder to accelerate. The exact cancellation of gravitational and inertial mass means free-fall acceleration is universal — a fact so profound it became the foundation of Einstein's general relativity.

subject: physics
question_text: When one bulb in your home burns out, all the other lights and appliances keep working normally. What does this tell you about how household circuits are wired, and why is that choice made?
_answer: Appliances are wired in parallel — each gets the full supply voltage on its own independent branch, so one device failing (an open branch) doesn't interrupt current through the others.
_explanation: In series wiring a single break stops everything and devices must share the voltage. Parallel wiring gives every appliance the same rated voltage, lets each be switched independently, and confines any failure to its own branch — which is why it is the universal choice for domestic circuits.

subject: physics
question_text: On a clear night, stars twinkle noticeably while planets shine with a steady light. Both are seen through the same turbulent atmosphere — why the difference?
_answer: A star is effectively a point source, so fluctuating atmospheric refraction randomly shifts and dims its single beam; a planet is an extended source of many points whose independent twinklings average out to steady light.
_explanation: Turbulent air layers of varying density continuously bend starlight by changing amounts, making the point image dance and flicker. A planet's disc subtends a finite angle, so it acts as many point sources whose fluctuations are uncorrelated and cancel on average, smoothing out the twinkle.

subject: physics
question_text: A quantity is calculated by multiplying two measured lengths together. The relative error in the result turns out to be the sum of the two relative errors — even though you multiplied, not added, the lengths. Why do the fractional errors add?
_answer: For a product z = xy, differentiation gives dz/z = dx/x + dy/y, so fractional errors add regardless of multiplication or division; the worst case assumes they reinforce.
_explanation: When quantities are multiplied or divided, their relative (fractional) errors combine additively, not their absolute errors. This follows because a small fractional change in each factor produces a fractional change in the product equal to their sum, and error analysis takes the worst case where they add.

subject: physics
question_text: In the measurement 0.00302 kg, the three zeros just after the decimal point do not count as significant figures, but the zero between the 3 and the 2 does. Why are some zeros significant and others not?
_answer: Leading zeros are mere placeholders fixing the decimal position and carry no measured information; a zero between nonzero digits was actually measured, so 0.00302 has three significant figures.
_explanation: Significant figures reflect the precision actually measured. Zeros that only locate the decimal point (leading zeros) are scale markers, not measurements, whereas a zero trapped between nonzero digits represents a genuine measured value and therefore counts.

subject: physics
question_text: Dimensional analysis can check an equation and even reveal how quantities depend on one another, yet it can never tell you the value of a pure number like ½ or 2π that might appear. Why is it blind to such constants?
_answer: Dimensionless constants have no units, so multiplying a formula by any of them leaves its dimensions unchanged; dimensional analysis only tracks units and cannot detect factors it cannot 'see'.
_explanation: The method follows how units combine and nothing more, so any pure numerical multiplier is invisible to it. That is why dimensional analysis can give the form of a relationship but never the numerical constants, which must come from experiment or a full derivation.

subject: physics
question_text: The area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement, but where the graph dips below the time axis, that area is counted as negative. What physical situation does the negative area represent?
_concept: signed area under a velocity-time graph
_answer: Negative velocity — motion in the negative direction — so that portion of area subtracts from displacement (though it still adds to total distance travelled).
_explanation: Displacement is the net signed area under the v-t curve. Intervals with negative velocity move the object opposite to the chosen positive direction, so their area is subtracted; distance travelled, by contrast, counts the magnitude of every area.

subject: physics
question_text: Sitting in a train that is moving forward, you glance at a train on the next track and it appears to be sliding backward, even though it too is genuinely moving forward. How can a forward-moving train look like it is going backward?
_answer: Your train is moving forward faster than the other; relative to your frame the slower train's velocity (its speed minus yours) is negative, so it appears to move backward.
_explanation: You perceive the other train's velocity relative to your own. When your forward speed exceeds the other train's, subtracting your velocity leaves a net backward relative velocity, making a genuinely forward-moving train appear to drift backward.

subject: physics
question_text: For an object starting from rest and accelerating uniformly, the distances it covers in successive equal time intervals are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 and so on. Why do these odd numbers appear?
_answer: Total distance from rest goes as t², and the differences between consecutive squares (1,4,9,16 → 1,3,5,7) are the consecutive odd numbers.
_explanation: With s ∝ t², cumulative distances after equal time steps are proportional to 1,4,9,16… The distance covered in each new interval is the difference between successive squares, and consecutive squares always differ by consecutive odd numbers, giving the 1:3:5:7 pattern.

subject: physics
question_text: Two forces act on a body. Is it possible for their resultant to be smaller in magnitude than either individual force, and if so, under what condition?
_concept: vector addition and resultant magnitude range
_answer: Yes — when the angle between them is large enough (obtuse), partial cancellation makes the resultant smaller than one or both; the resultant ranges from |A−B| to A+B.
_explanation: The magnitude of the sum of two vectors depends on the angle between them, spanning from |A−B| when antiparallel to A+B when parallel. For sufficiently large angles the vectors partly oppose, so the resultant can be smaller than either — reaching its minimum |A−B| when they point opposite ways.

subject: physics
question_text: To cross a flowing river in the shortest possible time, should a swimmer head straight across toward the far bank, or angle upstream against the current? (Assume constant swimming speed.)
_concept: relative velocity — shortest time river crossing
_answer: Head straight across — crossing time depends only on the velocity component perpendicular to the flow, which is maximized by pointing straight across; angling upstream diverts speed against the current and lengthens the time.
_explanation: Time to cross equals the river's width divided by the swimmer's velocity component perpendicular to the banks. Aiming straight across devotes the full swimming speed to that component, minimizing time, whereas angling upstream wastes effort fighting the current and increases crossing time (though it reduces downstream drift).

subject: physics
question_text: You are walking forward through rain that is falling perfectly vertically. To stay driest you must tilt your umbrella forward, into the direction you are moving. Why forward and not straight up or backward?
_answer: In your frame the rain has a backward horizontal relative velocity equal to your walking speed, so it appears to come from the front-above; tilting forward faces the umbrella into this apparent direction.
_explanation: Relative to a moving person, the rain's velocity is its downward velocity combined with the reverse of the person's velocity, giving a slanted approach from the front. The umbrella must be tilted toward that apparent source — forward — to intercept the rain.

subject: physics
question_text: Airbags and bending your knees when you land don't reduce the total momentum your body must lose — so how do they actually protect you from injury?
_answer: They extend the time over which the momentum change occurs; since average force equals momentum change divided by time, a longer stopping time means a smaller peak force on the body.
_explanation: The impulse (change in momentum) is fixed by your speed and mass. Spreading that impulse over a longer time reduces the average and peak force, and it is the force — not the momentum change itself — that causes injury, so cushioning lowers the damaging force.

subject: physics
