question_text: A horse pulls a cart. By Newton's third law the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal and opposite force. If these forces are equal and opposite, how does the horse-cart system move forward at all?
_concept: net external force on a system versus internal action-reaction pairs
_answer: The horse-cart forces act on different objects and cancel only within the system; the system accelerates because the ground's forward friction on the horse's hooves exceeds the backward drag, giving a net external force.
_explanation: Treating the horse and cart as one system, the internal action-reaction pair cancels, but motion depends on external forces. The forward friction the ground exerts on the horse pushes the whole system ahead, so the net external force — not the internal pair — determines the motion.

subject: physics
question_text: On a properly banked curve, a car can safely round the bend even on perfectly frictionless ice, as long as it travels at the design speed. How can it turn a corner with no friction at all?
_answer: The banked surface tilts the normal force so it points partly inward; its horizontal component supplies the centripetal force mv²/r, so no friction is needed at the design speed.
_explanation: Banking angles the road so that the normal force has an inward horizontal component. At the design speed this component exactly provides the required centripetal force, letting the car corner without friction — friction is only needed to cope with speeds different from the design value.

subject: physics
question_text: Push gently on a heavy crate and it doesn't budge; push a little harder and it still doesn't move. Somehow the friction matched each different push exactly. How does static friction 'know' how hard to push back?
_answer: Static friction is a self-adjusting reaction that grows to match the applied force up to a maximum (μ_s N); below that limit it exactly balances whatever force you apply, keeping net force zero.
_explanation: Unlike kinetic friction, static friction has no fixed value; it takes whatever magnitude is needed to prevent slipping, up to its limiting value μ_s N. Only when your push exceeds that ceiling does the crate break free and begin to slide.

subject: physics
question_text: Doubling a car's speed makes its braking distance four times longer, not just twice as long. Why does stopping distance grow with the square of the speed?
_answer: Kinetic energy is proportional to v², and the brakes must dissipate all of it through a roughly constant friction force over the stopping distance; since work = force × distance, distance is proportional to v².
_explanation: Braking removes kinetic energy by friction doing work Fd. With F approximately constant, the distance needed is proportional to the kinetic energy, which scales as v². So doubling speed quadruples the braking distance — a key reason speed limits matter so much.

subject: physics
question_text: When you throw a ball straight up, gravity does negative work on it going up and positive work coming down. What does the sign of the work tell you about the ball's kinetic energy in each phase?
_concept: work-energy theorem and sign of work
_answer: Negative work removes kinetic energy (the ball slows on the way up); positive work adds kinetic energy (it speeds up on the way down); by the work-energy theorem net work equals the change in kinetic energy.
_explanation: Work done by a force equals the change in kinetic energy it causes. Upward motion opposes gravity, so gravity's work is negative and kinetic energy falls; downward motion is along gravity, so its work is positive and kinetic energy rises.

subject: physics
question_text: Lift a book to a shelf straight up, or carry it there along a long winding path around the room — gravity does exactly the same total work either way. What property of gravity makes the path irrelevant?
_answer: Gravity is a conservative force, so the work it does depends only on the start and end heights, not the path; W = −mgΔh regardless of the route taken.
_explanation: For conservative forces such as gravity, the work done around any closed loop is zero, which makes the work between two points independent of the path. Only the net change in height matters, so the winding route and the straight lift require the same gravitational work.

subject: physics
question_text: Two motors both lift the same load to the same height, so they do the same amount of work — yet one is rated at a higher power. What does the higher power rating actually give you?
_answer: Speed — power is the rate of doing work, so the higher-power motor completes the same task in less time; the total energy expended is the same.
_explanation: Work (energy) depends only on force and distance, which are identical for both motors. Power is work divided by time, so a more powerful motor performs the identical job more quickly, even though both consume the same total energy apart from losses.

subject: physics
question_text: It is far easier to push a heavy door open by pushing near its outer edge than by pushing near the hinges. Why does the same force do more when applied farther from the hinge?
_chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
_answer: Torque equals force times the perpendicular distance from the axis, so pushing farther from the hinge increases the lever arm and hence the turning effect for the same force.
_explanation: Rotation is governed by torque, not force alone. Increasing the perpendicular distance from the axis multiplies the force's turning effect, which is exactly why door handles are placed as far from the hinges as possible.

subject: physics
question_text: A diver leaves the board rotating slowly, tucks into a tight ball to spin rapidly, then opens up to slow down before entering the water. No external torque acts during the dive — how does the diver control the spin rate?
_chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
_concept: conservation of angular momentum via body shape
_answer: By conserving angular momentum L = Iω: tucking reduces the moment of inertia so ω rises; extending increases I so ω falls.
_explanation: In the air the only force is gravity acting at the centre of mass, giving no torque about it, so angular momentum is conserved. Changing body shape redistributes mass relative to the rotation axis, trading moment of inertia against angular speed to spin faster or slower at will.

subject: physics
question_text: For a wheel rolling along the ground without slipping, one point on the wheel is momentarily at rest at every instant. Which point is it, and why isn't it moving even though the wheel clearly is?
_chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
_concept: instantaneous point of contact in rolling
_answer: The point touching the ground — its forward translational velocity and its backward rotational velocity (both equal to ωR) cancel exactly, so it is instantaneously at rest.
_explanation: In pure rolling the bottom point's rotational velocity points backward with magnitude ωR, exactly cancelling the wheel's forward velocity v = ωR. That momentary zero velocity is why rolling friction can be static, and it also makes the top of the wheel move at twice the centre's speed.

subject: physics
question_text: Every point on a spinning rigid disc takes the same time to complete one turn, so they all share the same angular velocity — yet a point on the rim moves much faster than one near the centre. How can the same rotation produce different speeds?
_chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
_concept: relation between linear and angular velocity
_answer: Linear speed v = ωr, so with a common angular velocity ω the points farther from the axis (larger r) move proportionally faster.
_explanation: Angular velocity describes how fast the angle sweeps, which is identical for all points of a rigid body. But the actual distance travelled per revolution is 2πr, larger for outer points, so their linear speed v = ωr grows with distance from the axis.

subject: physics
question_text: A geostationary satellite appears fixed over one spot on Earth permanently. Why must such a satellite orbit exactly above the equator, and why exactly with a 24-hour period?
_answer: To stay above a fixed point it must match Earth's rotation (about 24 h) and orbit in a plane through Earth's centre; only an equatorial orbit keeps it over a fixed latitude — any tilt would make it drift north-south.
_explanation: A satellite's orbital plane must pass through Earth's centre, so a stationary sub-satellite point is possible only over the equator. Matching the 24-hour rotation period (which fixes the orbital radius by Kepler's third law) then keeps the satellite motionless relative to the ground.

subject: physics
question_text: Counterintuitively, a satellite in a higher orbit moves more slowly than one in a lower orbit, even though it possesses more total energy. Why does orbiting higher mean moving slower?
_answer: Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) decreases as r increases because weaker gravity farther out needs less speed to supply the centripetal force; the extra total energy goes into potential energy, not speed.
_explanation: For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force, giving v = √(GM/r), which falls with distance. A higher satellite has greater total energy (largely potential), but its orbital speed is lower and its period longer.

subject: physics
question_text: A comet moves fastest when it is closest to the Sun and slowest when it is farthest away. What conserved quantity forces it to speed up and slow down like this?
_concept: Kepler's second law and angular momentum
_answer: Angular momentum — gravity acts along the line to the Sun and exerts no torque, so L is conserved, requiring larger speed at smaller distance; this is Kepler's law of equal areas.
_explanation: Because the gravitational force points straight at the Sun, it produces no torque about the Sun and the comet's angular momentum stays constant. To keep the product of speed and distance fixed, the comet must move faster at perihelion and slower at aphelion, sweeping equal areas in equal times.

subject: physics
question_text: Ocean tides produce two high-tide bulges — one on the side of Earth facing the Moon and, surprisingly, one on the far side away from it. Why is there a bulge on the side pointing away from the Moon?
_answer: Tides arise from differences in the Moon's gravity across Earth: the near side is pulled more than the centre, and the centre more than the far side, so relative to Earth's centre the far-side water is 'left behind' and bulges outward.
_explanation: The Moon's gravity weakens with distance, acting unequally on the near side, the centre, and the far side of Earth. Working in Earth's frame, this differential pull stretches the oceans on both the near and far sides, producing two bulges and roughly two high tides per day.

subject: physics
question_text: A thick steel cable can support a far heavier load than a thin one of the same steel before snapping, yet engineers say both fail at the same 'breaking stress'. How can the safe load differ if the breaking stress is identical?
_answer: Breaking stress (force per unit area) is a material property, so the maximum force equals breaking stress times cross-sectional area; a thicker cable has more area and therefore holds more force at the same breaking stress.
_explanation: Materials fail at a characteristic stress, not a characteristic force. Since stress is force divided by area, a larger cross-section can carry a proportionally larger force before reaching that same limiting stress — which is why load capacity scales with thickness.

subject: physics
question_text: For a wire obeying Hooke's law, the elastic energy stored when it is stretched equals only half of (stretching force × extension), not the full product. Where did the other half go?
_concept: elastic potential energy in a stretched wire
_answer: Nothing is lost — the restoring force builds up gradually from zero to its final value as the wire stretches, so the work done is the average force (half the maximum) times the extension: ½ × F × extension.
_explanation: Because the restoring force grows linearly with extension, it is not at its maximum during the whole stretch. Integrating force over extension gives the area of a triangle, ½Fx, which is the stored elastic potential energy — the factor of one-half is intrinsic, not a loss.

subject: physics
question_text: Stretch a rubber band along its length and it becomes noticeably thinner across its width. Why does pulling a material in one direction make it shrink in the perpendicular directions?
_answer: The Poisson effect — most materials tend to conserve volume, so elongating along one axis is accompanied by lateral contraction; the ratio of lateral to longitudinal strain is Poisson's ratio.
_explanation: When a material is stretched, its atoms move apart along the pull but draw slightly closer in the transverse directions to partly preserve volume. This accompanying lateral contraction is quantified by Poisson's ratio, a characteristic constant of the material.

subject: physics
question_text: A steel sewing needle is far denser than water, yet if placed very gently it can rest on the water's surface without sinking. What holds it up, since it clearly isn't buoyancy?
_concept: surface tension supporting a dense object
_answer: Surface tension — the water surface behaves like a stretched elastic film that deforms under the needle and pushes up; the needle rests on this film rather than displacing its own weight in water.
_explanation: Cohesive forces between surface molecules give the water surface a tension that resists being pierced. A gently placed needle depresses but doesn't break this film, and the upward vertical components of surface tension along its length support its weight — which is why a drop of detergent, lowering surface tension, sinks it.

subject: physics
question_text: During a violent storm, roofs are sometimes lifted off houses even when the wind is blowing horizontally across the top rather than upward. What force lifts the roof?
_answer: Fast wind over the roof lowers the pressure above it (Bernoulli's principle) while the still air inside stays at higher pressure; the upward pressure difference pushes the roof off.
_explanation: By Bernoulli's principle, higher air speed corresponds to lower pressure. Rapid airflow across the roof drops the pressure on top below the pressure of the calm air beneath, and this net upward pressure difference can exceed the roof's weight and lift it away.

subject: physics
question_text: A raindrop falling from a great height does not keep speeding up and hit the ground at bullet speed; instead it reaches a steady 'terminal' velocity. What stops it from accelerating further?
_answer: Air drag increases with speed until it balances gravity; when the upward drag equals the weight, the net force is zero and the drop falls at a constant terminal velocity.
_explanation: As the drop speeds up, viscous drag and air resistance grow with velocity. At terminal velocity the retarding force exactly cancels the weight, so the acceleration becomes zero and the drop descends at a constant, survivable speed instead of accelerating without limit.

subject: physics
question_text: Pour water into vessels of very different shapes and widths but fill each to the same height, and the pressure at the bottom is identical in every vessel, regardless of how much water each holds. Why doesn't the shape or amount of water matter?
_answer: Fluid pressure at a depth depends only on the depth, density, and gravity (P = ρgh), not on the container's shape or the total quantity of liquid.
_explanation: Pressure in a static fluid is determined by the vertical depth beneath the surface, since it reflects the weight of the fluid column per unit area directly above. Slanting walls provide extra support forces, so at equal depth the bottom pressure is the same whether the vessel is wide or narrow — the hydrostatic paradox.

subject: physics
question_text: In a freezing lake, fish survive the winter near the bottom, where the water stays around 4°C while ice forms on the surface. What unusual property of water makes the bottom the warmest place?
_answer: Water is densest at about 4°C (anomalous expansion), so 4°C water sinks to the bottom while colder, less dense water and ice float on top, insulating the liquid below.
_explanation: Unlike most liquids, water contracts as it cools to 4°C and then expands on further cooling. The densest 4°C water settles at the bottom and ice (less dense than water) forms on the surface, allowing aquatic life to survive in the liquid layer beneath.

subject: physics
question_text: During the day a cool breeze blows from the sea toward the land, and at night the flow reverses, blowing from land to sea. Why does the coast 'breathe' in and out like this?
_answer: Water has a much higher specific heat than land, so by day land heats faster, the warm air over it rises, and cool sea air flows in; at night land cools faster, the air over the warmer sea rises, and the breeze reverses.
_explanation: Land's low specific heat lets it warm and cool quickly, while the sea's high specific heat keeps its temperature steadier. The resulting temperature and pressure differences drive air from the cooler surface toward the warmer one, reversing direction between day and night.

subject: physics
question_text: On a cold morning a metal railing feels much colder than a wooden bench right beside it, even though both are at exactly the same temperature. Why does the metal feel colder?
_concept: thermal conductivity and sensation of cold
_answer: Metal is a far better thermal conductor, so it draws heat out of your hand much faster than wood; the feeling of cold is really the rate of heat loss, not the object's temperature.
_explanation: Your skin judges 'cold' by how quickly heat leaves it. Metal's high conductivity conducts heat away rapidly, while wood conducts slowly, so despite being at the same temperature the metal feels much colder to the touch.

subject: physics
question_text: A tiny cup of boiling water and a huge tank of lukewarm water are placed in contact. The tank holds far more total heat energy, yet heat flows from the small hot cup into the large tank. Why does heat flow from the object with less total energy?
_answer: Heat flows according to temperature difference, not total energy content; it always moves from higher to lower temperature, so the hotter cup loses heat to the cooler tank despite the tank's larger energy.
_explanation: The direction of spontaneous heat flow is set by temperature, which measures average energy per molecule, not the total thermal energy. The boiling cup is at a higher temperature, so energy flows out of it into the cooler but larger tank until their temperatures equalize.

subject: physics
question_text: Spray from a deodorant or aerosol can feels cold on your skin, and the can itself grows cooler as you use it. What thermodynamic process cools the escaping gas?
_answer: Adiabatic expansion — the gas expands rapidly against the outside pressure with little time to exchange heat, doing work at the expense of its internal energy, so its temperature drops.
_explanation: When the compressed gas escapes and expands quickly, there is almost no time for heat to flow in, making the process nearly adiabatic. The gas does work pushing back the atmosphere using its own internal energy, and since internal energy falls, so does temperature — the same principle behind cloud formation in rising air.

subject: physics
question_text: A gas is taken from state A to state B by two completely different processes; one absorbs much more heat than the other. Yet the change in internal energy is identical for both. Why doesn't the route matter for internal energy?
_concept: internal energy as a state function
_answer: Internal energy is a state function depending only on the state (for an ideal gas, its temperature), so ΔU depends only on the endpoints; heat and work differ by path, but their difference Q − W = ΔU is fixed.
_explanation: Unlike heat and work, which are path-dependent, internal energy depends solely on the current state of the system. Different processes exchange different amounts of heat and work, but the first law forces Q − W to equal the same ΔU set by the initial and final states.

subject: physics
question_text: In a complete thermodynamic cycle a gas returns exactly to its starting state, so its internal energy is unchanged. Yet an engine running this cycle still delivers useful work each time round. Where does that work come from if internal energy hasn't changed?
_answer: From heat — over a cycle ΔU = 0, so the first law gives net work equal to net heat absorbed; the engine converts the heat taken in (minus heat rejected) into work each cycle.
_explanation: Returning to the same state means no change in internal energy, so the net heat absorbed equals the net work done. The engine takes in heat from a hot source and rejects some to a cold sink, and the difference emerges as useful work every cycle — how all heat engines run.

subject: physics
question_text: On a pressure-volume graph, the curve for an adiabatic change is always steeper than the isothermal curve passing through the same point. Why does insulating the gas make its P-V curve steeper?
_answer: In adiabatic expansion the gas also cools (no heat added), so its pressure falls faster than in the isothermal case where temperature is held constant; the adiabatic slope is γ times the isothermal slope.
_explanation: During isothermal expansion, heat flows in to keep the temperature and pressure support up. Adiabatically, the gas loses internal energy as it expands and cools, so its pressure drops more rapidly for the same increase in volume, making the adiabat steeper by the factor γ = Cp/Cv.

subject: physics
question_text: Gas molecules travel at hundreds of metres per second, yet a whiff of perfume takes many seconds to drift across a still room. Why is the smell so slow if the molecules are so fast?
_answer: Diffusion is slow because each molecule follows a zig-zag path, colliding billions of times per second (short mean free path); its net displacement grows far more slowly than the total distance it travels.
_explanation: Between collisions a molecule moves fast, but it constantly collides and changes direction at random. This random walk means the perfume molecule's net progress across the room is tiny compared with the total path length, so the scent spreads slowly despite the high molecular speeds.

subject: physics
question_text: Gas pressure in a container presses equally on the bottom, the sides, and the top. Why isn't the pressure greater at the bottom, the way it is deep in a liquid or under a stack of books?
_concept: molecular random motion and isotropic pressure
_answer: Gas molecules move randomly in all directions with the same average speed, so they strike every wall equally often and hard; gravity's effect on such light, fast molecules is negligible over ordinary container sizes.
_explanation: Gas pressure arises from random molecular impacts, which have no preferred direction, so it acts equally on all surfaces. The weight of the gas creates only a minuscule pressure gradient with height, unlike a liquid, so for a normal container the pressure is effectively uniform in every direction.

subject: physics
question_text: As a gas is cooled its molecules move slower and slower, and absolute zero is defined as the temperature at which this motion would essentially stop. Why can nothing be cooled below this temperature?
_concept: absolute zero as the lower limit of temperature
_answer: Temperature measures molecular kinetic energy, which cannot be negative; at absolute zero (classically) all translational motion ceases, so there is no lower temperature possible.
_explanation: Since kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature and can never be less than zero, the point where molecular motion classically halts sets the lowest possible temperature. You can approach absolute zero but never reach it, and nothing can be colder because there is no more energy to remove.

subject: physics
question_text: A pendulum clock that keeps perfect time in winter runs slightly slow during hot summer weather. Why does warmth make the clock lose time?
_answer: Heat expands the pendulum rod, increasing its length; since the period T = 2π√(L/g) grows with L, each swing takes longer and the clock runs slow.
_explanation: A longer pendulum has a longer period. Thermal expansion in summer lengthens the rod slightly, increasing the time per oscillation, so fewer swings occur per real second and the clock falls behind.

subject: physics
question_text: A real pendulum's swings gradually shrink and eventually stop, but the time taken for each swing stays almost the same the whole way. Why does the amplitude fade while the period barely changes?
_answer: Damping from air resistance and friction removes energy each cycle, so the amplitude decays roughly exponentially; but the period of SHM doesn't depend on amplitude, so for light damping it is nearly unchanged.
_explanation: Resistive forces steadily drain the oscillator's energy, shrinking the amplitude over time. Because the period of simple harmonic motion is independent of amplitude (and only slightly altered by light damping), the swings get smaller while keeping nearly the same timing until motion ceases.

subject: physics
question_text: Watch a point moving steadily around a circle, but view it edge-on so you see only its shadow projected onto a wall. The shadow moves back and forth in perfect simple harmonic motion. Why does uniform circular motion project into SHM?
_concept: SHM as projection of uniform circular motion
_answer: The projection of uniform circular motion onto a diameter varies as a sine or cosine of time, which is exactly the equation of simple harmonic motion.
_explanation: A point on a circle has coordinates that vary sinusoidally as the angle increases uniformly. Projecting onto one axis discards the perpendicular component, leaving x = A cos(ωt) — the definition of SHM — which is why the shadow oscillates harmonically.

subject: physics
question_text: In a mass oscillating on a spring, the kinetic energy and the potential energy each rise and fall twice during a single full oscillation of the mass. Why does the energy cycle at double the frequency of the motion?
_concept: energy in SHM oscillates at twice the frequency
_answer: Energy depends on the square of displacement or velocity, and squaring a sinusoid of frequency f produces a term at 2f, so kinetic and potential energy each peak twice per oscillation.
_explanation: The mass reaches maximum displacement twice per cycle (both extremes) and passes through the centre at full speed twice per cycle. Since energies go as position² or velocity², they peak twice per oscillation, giving them double the frequency of the displacement.

subject: physics
question_text: A pipe closed at one end produces a fundamental note an octave lower than an identical pipe open at both ends, and it is missing the even harmonics. Why does closing one end change both the pitch and the harmonics?
_concept: standing waves in closed versus open pipes
_answer: A closed end forces a displacement node and the open end an antinode, so the fundamental fits only a quarter wavelength (versus half for an open pipe), halving the frequency; the boundary conditions allow only odd harmonics.
_explanation: Standing-wave patterns must have a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. This makes the longest fitting wavelength four times the pipe length (twice the length for an open pipe), lowering the fundamental by an octave and permitting only odd multiples of it.

subject: physics
question_text: During an earthquake, some seismic waves pass right through Earth's liquid outer core while another type is completely blocked by it. Why can a liquid transmit one kind of wave but not the other?
_answer: Liquids and gases have no shear rigidity, so they cannot support transverse (shear/S) waves, which are blocked, but they do transmit longitudinal (pressure/P) waves.
_explanation: Transverse waves require a medium that resists shearing, a property only solids possess. Fluids can be compressed, so they carry longitudinal P-waves, but they simply flow under shear, so S-waves cannot propagate through the liquid outer core — evidence that first revealed the core is molten.

subject: physics
question_text: A loudspeaker sounds four times weaker in intensity when you double your distance from it, not just twice as weak. Why does sound intensity fall as the square of the distance?
_answer: The emitted energy spreads over a spherical wavefront whose area grows as 4πr², so intensity (power per unit area) falls as 1/r²; doubling the distance quarters the intensity.
_explanation: A point source radiates its energy uniformly over expanding spheres. Since the same power is spread over an area proportional to r², the intensity is inversely proportional to r², making both sound and light fall off as the inverse square of distance.

subject: physics
question_text: Pluck a guitar string at its centre and it sounds mellow; pluck it near the bridge and it sounds bright and twangy — the same string playing the same note. Why does the plucking position change the tone?
_answer: The plucking position sets which harmonics are excited and how strongly; plucking at the centre favours the fundamental and suppresses certain harmonics (mellow), while plucking near the end excites many higher harmonics (bright).
_explanation: A string vibrates as a mixture of harmonics whose amplitudes depend on where it is displaced. Plucking at a point emphasizes harmonics that have large motion there and misses those with a node there, so the harmonic recipe — and thus the timbre — changes with plucking position even though the pitch stays the same.

subject: physics
question_text: Electric charge always comes in whole-number multiples of the electron's charge — you can have one or two electrons' worth of charge but never one-and-a-half. Why is charge 'quantized' like this?
_answer: Charge is carried by discrete particles (electrons, protons), each with a fixed elementary charge e, so any net charge must be an integer multiple ne of that unit.
_explanation: Since matter is built from charged particles carrying fixed charge ±e, transferring charge means moving whole particles. There is no way to move a fraction of an electron in ordinary processes, so observable charge is always an integer multiple of e — the quantization of charge.

subject: physics
question_text: Charge accumulates most densely at the sharpest points and edges of a charged conductor, which is exactly why lightning rods are made pointed. Why does charge crowd onto sharp points?
_concept: charge density and field at sharp points
_answer: On a charged conductor the surface charge density is highest where the curvature is greatest, producing the strongest field there; this intense field ionizes nearby air, letting a pointed rod discharge or intercept strikes.
_explanation: Keeping a conductor's surface at a single potential requires more charge per unit area where the surface curves sharply. The resulting very strong field at points can ionize surrounding air (corona discharge), which is why pointed rods are so effective at collecting or releasing charge.

subject: physics
question_text: Just outside the surface of a charged conductor in equilibrium, the electric field always points exactly perpendicular to the surface, never at a slant. Why can't the field have a component along the surface?
_concept: field is normal to a conductor surface
_answer: Any tangential component would push the conductor's free charges sideways, causing currents; in electrostatic equilibrium the charges are at rest, so the tangential field must be zero, leaving only the perpendicular component.
_explanation: Free charges on a conductor rearrange until they feel no force along the surface. A surviving tangential field would keep moving them, contradicting equilibrium, so just outside the conductor the field must be entirely normal to the surface.

subject: physics
question_text: Place an electric dipole in a uniform electric field and it experiences a turning effect but no overall push in any direction. Why does the field twist the dipole without moving it as a whole?
_concept: dipole in a uniform field: torque without net force
_answer: The equal and opposite charges feel equal and opposite forces in a uniform field, giving zero net force but a couple (torque) that tends to align the dipole with the field.
_explanation: In a uniform field both ends of the dipole feel the same magnitude of force in opposite directions, so the forces cancel for translation. Because they act at different points, they form a couple that produces a torque, rotating the dipole toward alignment with the field.

subject: physics
question_text: Moving a charge from one point to another along an equipotential surface requires zero work, no matter how long the path taken. Why is no work done even on a long journey across such a surface?
_concept: no work along an equipotential surface
_answer: Work equals charge times potential difference, and every point on an equipotential surface has the same potential, so ΔV = 0 and W = 0; equivalently, the field is perpendicular to the surface, so the force does no work along it.
_explanation: An equipotential surface has a constant potential throughout, so moving between any two of its points involves no potential difference and therefore no work. Equivalently, the electric field is everywhere perpendicular to the surface, so any displacement along it is perpendicular to the force.

subject: physics
question_text: Connect two capacitors of very different values in series across a battery, and both end up holding exactly the same charge. Why must capacitors in series carry equal charge?
_answer: The plates between the two capacitors form an isolated conductor that started neutral, so charge +Q on one facing plate induces −Q on the other; conservation of charge forces every capacitor in the series to carry the same Q.
_explanation: In a series chain the inner plates form an isolated system that was initially neutral. Charge merely redistributes within it, so whatever charge appears on one capacitor's plate induces an equal and opposite charge on its neighbour, giving identical charge on each capacitor regardless of their capacitances.

subject: physics
question_text: Sliding an insulating sheet of glass or plastic between the plates of a capacitor increases its capacitance, letting it store more charge at the same voltage. How does an insulator boost the capacitance?
_concept: effect of a dielectric on capacitance
_answer: The dielectric polarizes, creating an internal field opposing the applied field and reducing the net field (and voltage) between the plates; with V lowered for the same charge, C = Q/V rises by the dielectric constant K.
_explanation: Molecules in the dielectric align to produce bound surface charges whose field partly cancels the plates' field. For a given charge this lowers the potential difference across the capacitor, and since capacitance is charge divided by voltage, reducing V increases C by the factor K.

subject: physics
question_text: When a capacitor is charged, energy is stored — but where exactly does that energy reside, given that the region between the plates is essentially empty space?
_concept: energy stored in the electric field
_answer: In the electric field itself — the energy is distributed throughout the region where the field exists, with an energy density proportional to E² (½ε₀E²), rather than sitting on the plates or in the wires.
_explanation: Modern physics locates the stored energy in the electric field filling the space between the plates. The energy per unit volume is ½ε₀E², so the total energy depends on the field strength and the volume it occupies — the same idea that lets electromagnetic waves carry energy through empty space.

subject: physics
question_text: A bird can perch safely on a bare high-voltage power line, but a person touching the same line while standing on the ground is electrocuted. Why is the bird unharmed?
_answer: Current flows only when there is a potential difference across the body; the bird's feet are close together on one wire and thus at nearly the same potential, so negligible current flows through it.
_explanation: Electrocution requires a potential difference to drive current through the body. The bird's feet share almost the same potential on one wire, so there is essentially no voltage across it and no path to ground, whereas a person bridging the wire and the ground experiences the full voltage and a large current.

subject: physics
question_text: At any junction in a circuit, the total current flowing in equals the total current flowing out — none piles up. What fundamental conservation law does this rule express?
_concept: Kirchhoff's junction rule and charge conservation
_answer: Conservation of electric charge — since charge is neither created nor destroyed nor accumulated at a junction in steady state, the currents in and out must balance.
_explanation: Kirchhoff's junction (current) rule is a direct statement of charge conservation. In a steady current, charge entering a node must leave it at the same rate, or charge would build up and the current would not be steady, so the algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero.

subject: physics
question_text: A fuse is deliberately made of a short, thin piece of wire that melts and breaks the circuit when the current gets too large. Why is the fuse made the thinnest, weakest part of the circuit on purpose?
_concept: heating effect of current and fuses
_answer: A thin wire has higher resistance and less mass, so it heats up (by I²R) and reaches its melting point before the rest of the wiring; it melts first, breaking the circuit and protecting the appliance from dangerous overcurrent.
_explanation: Heating in a wire goes as I²R, and a thin fuse concentrates this heating in a small, easily melted element. When the current exceeds the safe limit, the fuse melts and opens the circuit before the heavier house wiring can overheat and start a fire.

subject: physics
question_text: In a cyclotron, a charged particle spirals outward gaining energy, yet the time it takes to complete each loop stays exactly the same even as its speed and orbit radius grow. Why is the period constant?
_answer: The period T = 2πm/(qB) depends only on mass, charge, and field — not on speed or radius; as the speed rises the radius grows in proportion, so the time per revolution is unchanged (non-relativistically).
_explanation: For circular motion in a magnetic field the orbit radius and the speed increase together such that the time per orbit stays fixed. Because the period is independent of speed, the accelerating voltage can be applied at a constant frequency — the essential idea that makes the cyclotron work.

subject: physics
question_text: A stationary charge placed in a magnetic field feels no force at all, but the same charge feels a force the instant it begins to move. Why does a magnetic field act only on moving charges?
_answer: The magnetic force is F = qv×B, which is zero when v = 0; a magnetic field exerts force only on moving charges (currents), unlike an electric field, which acts on charges regardless of motion.
_explanation: Magnetic force depends on the charge's velocity through the cross product qv×B. With zero velocity the force vanishes, so a static charge is unaffected. Only when the charge moves does it act as a current element that the field can push sideways.

subject: physics
question_text: A current-carrying rectangular loop in a uniform magnetic field tends to rotate but is not pushed off in any direction — the basis of the electric motor. Why does the field rotate the loop rather than move it bodily?
_answer: Opposite sides of the loop carry current in opposite directions and feel equal and opposite forces (zero net force) that form a couple, producing a torque that rotates the loop.
_explanation: In a uniform field the net force on a closed current loop is zero because the forces on opposite sides cancel. Those forces act along different lines, however, so they create a torque that spins the loop toward alignment — the fundamental action driving electric motors and moving-coil galvanometers.

subject: physics
question_text: The magnetic field deep inside a long current-carrying solenoid is very uniform and depends only on the current and the number of turns per unit length — not on the solenoid's diameter. Why doesn't the width of the solenoid affect the field inside?
_answer: Ampère's law gives B = μ₀nI inside a long solenoid, depending only on turns per unit length n and current I; the contributions arrange so the interior field is uniform and independent of the diameter.
_explanation: For an ideal long solenoid the field outside is nearly zero and inside is uniform. Ampère's law relates the interior field only to the enclosed current per unit length, giving B = μ₀nI with no dependence on diameter, so a wide and a narrow solenoid with the same n and I have the same interior field.

subject: physics
question_text: Placed in a magnetic field, a diamagnetic material is weakly pushed away, a paramagnetic one is weakly pulled in, and a ferromagnetic one is strongly pulled in. What causes these three opposite responses?
_answer: Diamagnets have no permanent atomic moments and develop weak opposing moments (repelled); paramagnets have permanent moments that partially align with the field (weakly attracted); ferromagnets have strongly coupled domains that align powerfully (strongly attracted).
_explanation: The response depends on the atoms' magnetic moments. Induced opposing currents make diamagnets repel; randomly oriented permanent moments partly aligning make paramagnets weakly attract; and domain alignment through strong exchange coupling makes ferromagnets attract strongly and retain magnetization.

subject: physics
question_text: A freely suspended compass needle doesn't lie perfectly horizontal at most places — it tips at an angle to the horizontal, and this 'dip' angle changes with latitude. Why isn't Earth's magnetic field horizontal everywhere?
_concept: angle of dip and Earth's field
_answer: Earth's field resembles a giant tilted dipole whose lines emerge vertically near the magnetic poles and run horizontally near the magnetic equator, so a suspended needle dips by an angle that grows from the equator toward the poles.
_explanation: The geomagnetic field has both horizontal and vertical components whose ratio varies with latitude. Near the equator the field is almost horizontal (small dip), while near the poles it plunges steeply into the ground (large dip), because the dipole field lines curve from one pole to the other.

subject: physics
question_text: Electromagnets use a soft iron core, while permanent magnets are made from hard steel. Why is soft iron ideal for an electromagnet but useless as a permanent magnet?
_answer: Soft iron has high permeability and low retentivity/coercivity, so it magnetizes strongly when current flows but loses almost all its magnetism when the current stops — perfect for a switchable electromagnet but unable to stay permanently magnetized.
_explanation: An electromagnet needs a core that responds strongly to the coil's field and releases it on demand, which soft iron's easily reversed domains do well. A permanent magnet instead needs high retentivity to hold its magnetization, so hard magnetic materials, not soft iron, are used for them.

subject: physics
question_text: When you switch off a circuit containing a large coil, such as a motor or an electromagnet, a spark often jumps across the switch contacts. What causes this sudden spark at the moment of disconnection?
_answer: The coil's self-inductance opposes the sudden drop in current by inducing a large back-emf (L·dI/dt); the rapid change produces a high voltage that ionizes the air gap and causes a spark.
_explanation: An inductor resists changes in its own current. Opening the switch forces the current to fall almost instantly, making dI/dt enormous and inducing a large emf that tries to maintain the current — this high voltage arcs across the opening contacts as a spark.

subject: physics
question_text: Slide a metal rod along two parallel conducting rails inside a magnetic field, and a voltage appears across the rod that can drive a current. Where does this emf come from if there is no battery anywhere?
_answer: Motional emf — the magnetic force qv×B on the rod's free electrons pushes them along the rod, separating charge and producing an emf equal to BLv; the moving rod behaves like a battery.
_explanation: As the rod moves through the field, each free charge feels a magnetic force along the rod's length, driving charges to one end. This charge separation sets up an emf of magnitude BLv, so the mechanical work of moving the rod is converted into electrical energy — the basis of electric generators.

subject: physics
question_text: A changing current in one coil can induce a voltage in a completely separate, unconnected coil placed nearby. How does the second coil 'feel' the first with no electrical connection between them?
_answer: Through mutual inductance — the changing current in the first coil produces a changing magnetic flux that links the second coil, and by Faraday's law this changing flux induces an emf in it.
_explanation: The first coil's varying current creates a varying magnetic field, part of which threads the second coil. Faraday's law says a changing linked flux induces an emf, so the coils couple magnetically across empty space — the operating principle of transformers.

subject: physics
question_text: An AC generator produces a voltage that smoothly rises and falls as a sine wave even though its coil spins at a constant rate. Why does steady rotation produce a sinusoidally oscillating voltage?
_concept: origin of sinusoidal emf in a generator
_answer: The flux through the rotating coil varies as the cosine of the angle (Φ = BA cosθ), so the induced emf, being −dΦ/dt, varies as the sine of the angle; uniform rotation makes θ = ωt, giving a sinusoidal emf.
_explanation: As the coil turns, the magnetic flux threading it changes with the coil's orientation, following a cosine. Faraday's law gives an emf proportional to the rate of change of this flux, which for uniform rotation is a sine function — hence the smoothly alternating output.

subject: physics
question_text: Electric power is sent across long distances at extremely high voltages (hundreds of thousands of volts) and only stepped down near homes. Why transmit it at high voltage instead of the safer low voltage used indoors?
_answer: For a given power P = VI, higher voltage means lower current, and since transmission losses are I²R, reducing the current sharply cuts the energy wasted as heat in the lines.
_explanation: The power delivered equals voltage times current, so raising the voltage lets the same power flow with much less current. Because line losses scale as the square of the current, high-voltage transmission dramatically reduces wasted energy, and transformers then step the voltage down for safe household use.

subject: physics
question_text: Household mains is called '220 volts', but the voltage actually swings between roughly +311 V and −311 V many times each second. What does the single number 220 V represent?
_answer: 220 V is the root-mean-square (rms) value — the effective DC voltage that would deliver the same average power; for a sinusoid the rms equals the peak divided by √2, and 311/√2 ≈ 220.
_explanation: Because AC voltage constantly changes and averages to zero, we quote its rms value, which captures its power-delivering ability. The rms is the peak divided by √2, so a 311 V peak corresponds to 220 V rms — the value that heats a resistor like an equivalent 220 V DC source.

subject: physics
question_text: A pure inductor or a pure capacitor connected to an AC supply carries current continuously, yet consumes zero average power over a cycle. How can current flow without any power being used up?
_answer: In a pure inductor or capacitor the current is 90° out of phase with the voltage, so the average of the power (VI) over a cycle is zero — energy is alternately stored and returned to the source rather than dissipated.
_explanation: Average power depends on the phase angle between voltage and current through cosφ. For an ideal inductor or capacitor the phase difference is 90°, making cosφ = 0, so no net energy is consumed; the component borrows energy for part of the cycle and gives it back — a 'wattless' current.

subject: physics
question_text: In a DC circuit a coil of wire offers only its small ohmic resistance, but the same coil strongly limits an alternating current. Why does the coil oppose AC far more than DC?
_answer: For AC the coil adds inductive reactance X_L = ωL that grows with frequency, so its total opposition (impedance) far exceeds the mere resistance it shows to DC.
_explanation: A steady DC current sees only the wire's resistance, but an alternating current continuously changes, so the inductor's self-induced back-emf opposes it. This frequency-dependent reactance combines with resistance to give a much larger impedance for AC than for DC.

subject: physics
question_text: Radio waves, visible light, X-rays and gamma rays are all electromagnetic waves, yet they behave very differently and carry vastly different energies. What single property do they all share exactly in vacuum, and what makes them differ?
_answer: They all travel at the same speed c in vacuum; they differ in frequency (and wavelength), which determines their energy and how they interact with matter.
_explanation: Every electromagnetic wave is an oscillation of electric and magnetic fields propagating at c in vacuum, whatever its type. What distinguishes radio from gamma rays is frequency and wavelength — higher frequency means higher photon energy E = hf — but the vacuum speed is identical for all.

subject: physics
question_text: Sunlight contains visible light, harmless in normal amounts, and ultraviolet light, which causes sunburn and damages skin cells. Both are electromagnetic waves — why is ultraviolet so much more damaging than visible light?
_answer: Ultraviolet photons have higher frequency and thus higher energy (E = hf) than visible photons — enough to break chemical bonds and damage DNA — whereas lower-energy visible photons generally cannot.
_explanation: Photon energy rises with frequency, and ultraviolet lies just beyond violet with greater energy per photon. This extra energy lets UV photons ionize molecules and break the bonds in biological tissue, causing cellular damage that visible light's weaker photons cannot inflict.

subject: physics
question_text: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun, so much so that on the comet's outbound journey the tail can actually lead the way. What pushes the tail away from the Sun regardless of the comet's motion?
_concept: radiation pressure and momentum of light
_answer: Sunlight and the solar wind exert an outward radiation pressure (electromagnetic waves carry momentum), pushing the comet's released dust and gas away from the Sun no matter which way the comet is travelling.
_explanation: Electromagnetic radiation carries momentum, so absorbed or reflected sunlight pushes on the comet's dust and gas. This radiation pressure, aided by the solar wind, always drives the tail directly away from the Sun, which is why the tail can point ahead of the comet as it recedes.

subject: physics
question_text: The Sun is actually still below the horizon at the moment it appears to rise, and it has already set when we still see it at sunset. Why do we see the Sun before it truly rises and after it truly sets?
_answer: Atmospheric refraction bends the Sun's light downward as it passes through the denser lower air, so the Sun appears raised above its true position, letting us see it while it is geometrically below the horizon.
_explanation: Light from the Sun travels from thinner to denser air near the horizon and bends toward Earth. This bending lifts the Sun's apparent position by roughly its own diameter, so sunrise appears slightly early and sunset slightly late compared with the geometric horizon crossing.

subject: physics
question_text: Cars use convex mirrors for side and rear-view mirrors, and shops use them for security, even though the images they form are smaller than the objects. Why choose a mirror that shrinks the image?
_concept: convex mirror and field of view
_answer: A convex mirror always forms an erect, diminished, virtual image and gives a wide field of view, letting the driver see a large area behind in a small mirror — trading image size for coverage.
_explanation: Because a convex mirror diverges reflected rays, it captures light from a wide angle and compresses it into a small upright image. This expanded field of view is invaluable for spotting more traffic or a larger part of a store, outweighing the reduced image size — hence 'objects are closer than they appear'.

subject: physics
question_text: A glass lens has a fixed focal length in air, but submerge it in water and its focal length changes dramatically, while a mirror's focal length would not change at all. Why does a lens behave differently underwater but a mirror doesn't?
_concept: focal length, refraction, and the surrounding medium
_answer: A lens works by refraction, which depends on the refractive-index contrast between glass and its surroundings, so immersing it in water reduces that contrast and lengthens the focal length; a mirror works by reflection, which is independent of the medium.
_explanation: Refraction at the lens surfaces depends on the ratio of the glass and medium refractive indices. Water's index is close to glass's, so the bending weakens and the focal length increases. Reflection, which governs mirrors, doesn't depend on the surrounding index, so a mirror's focal length is the same in air or water.

subject: physics
question_text: On a hot day, a distant stretch of road looks like a shimmering pool of water, though there is no water there. What optical effect creates such a road or desert mirage?
_answer: Hot air near the ground is less dense (lower refractive index) than the cooler air above, so light from the sky bends gradually and undergoes total internal reflection, appearing to come up from the ground as a watery reflection.
_explanation: A temperature gradient makes the air's refractive index increase with height. Light heading downward is bent progressively until it turns back upward (total internal reflection), so the observer sees an inverted image of the sky on the road, which is mistaken for reflecting water.

subject: physics
question_text: Soap bubbles and thin films of oil on a wet road shimmer with rainbow colours even under plain white light. Where do the colours come from if the soap and oil are themselves colourless?
_answer: Thin-film interference — light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of the film interferes, and the path difference (set by the film's thickness and the viewing angle) makes different wavelengths interfere constructively at different places, producing colours.
_explanation: The two reflected waves from a thin film's surfaces recombine with a path difference that depends on the film thickness. For each thickness, certain wavelengths interfere constructively and others destructively, so white light is split into the shifting rainbow patterns seen on bubbles and oil slicks.

subject: physics
question_text: In a double-slit experiment, moving the slits closer together spreads the interference fringes farther apart, and red light gives wider fringes than blue light. What determines how widely spaced the fringes are?
_answer: Fringe width β = λD/d — it increases with wavelength λ and screen distance D and decreases with slit separation d, so closer slits and longer-wavelength (red) light give wider fringes.
_explanation: The spacing between bright fringes depends directly on the wavelength and the slit-to-screen distance and inversely on the separation between the slits. Reducing d or using red (longer λ) light widens the fringes, while blue light packs them closer — a direct signature of the wavelength.

subject: physics
question_text: The sky is blue during the day but turns red and orange at sunset — the same sunlight passing through the same air. What makes the sky change colour?
_answer: Air molecules scatter shorter (blue) wavelengths much more strongly than longer (red) ones (Rayleigh scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴), so the daytime sky glows blue; at sunset the long slanted path scatters away the blue, leaving the transmitted red and orange.
_explanation: Rayleigh scattering strongly favours short wavelengths, so blue light is scattered across the whole sky by day. Near sunset, sunlight travels through much more atmosphere, scattering out most of the blue before it reaches you, so the remaining directly transmitted light is dominated by red and orange.

subject: physics
question_text: For each metal there is a minimum frequency of light below which no electrons are ejected, no matter how long you shine the light. Why does each metal have its own threshold frequency?
_chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
_answer: Electrons are bound to the metal by an energy called the work function; only a photon with energy hf at least equal to the work function can free an electron, so the threshold frequency is the work function divided by h and differs from metal to metal.
_explanation: Freeing an electron requires at least the work function's worth of energy delivered in a single photon. Since different metals hold their electrons with different work functions, each has a distinct minimum (threshold) frequency below which no single photon is energetic enough to cause emission.

subject: physics
question_text: Light has no mass, yet a beam of light can exert a tiny push on a surface it strikes — the idea behind proposed 'solar sails'. How can massless light carry momentum?
_chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
_answer: A photon carries momentum p = h/λ = E/c despite having no rest mass; when light is absorbed or reflected it transfers this momentum, producing a small radiation pressure.
_explanation: In quantum theory a photon's momentum is related to its energy by p = E/c (equivalently h/λ), independent of mass. On striking a surface, photons deliver momentum just as particles would, creating a small but real pressure that could propel a lightweight solar sail.

subject: physics
question_text: In the photoelectric effect, electrons are emitted the instant light of sufficient frequency hits the metal, with no measurable delay, even for very dim light. Why was this immediate response impossible to explain with the wave theory of light?
_chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
_concept: instantaneous emission and the photon model
_answer: Wave theory predicts energy arrives spread out and would take time to accumulate enough to free an electron (especially for dim light), yet emission is instantaneous — explained instead by a single photon delivering all its energy hf to one electron at once.
_explanation: If light were purely a spread-out wave, a faint beam would need appreciable time to build up the energy to eject an electron. The observed instantaneous emission shows energy arrives in concentrated packets (photons), each able to eject an electron immediately if hf exceeds the work function.

subject: physics
question_text: Hydrogen's emission spectrum is not a single set of lines but several distinct groups lying in the ultraviolet, visible, and infrared. Why does hydrogen produce several separate series of lines?
_answer: Each series corresponds to electron transitions ending on a particular level: transitions down to n=1 give the ultraviolet Lyman series, to n=2 the visible Balmer series, to n=3 the infrared Paschen series, and so on.
_explanation: Photon energy equals the difference between the initial and final energy levels. Grouping transitions by their common final level produces distinct series with characteristic energy ranges — Lyman (to n=1), Balmer (to n=2), Paschen (to n=3) — explaining the several separate groups of lines.

subject: physics
question_text: It takes exactly 13.6 electron-volts to completely remove the electron from a hydrogen atom in its ground state. What does this particular number tell us about the atom's structure?
_answer: 13.6 eV is hydrogen's ground-state binding (ionization) energy — the energy needed to lift the electron from the n=1 level to being just free (n=∞); it equals the magnitude of the ground-state energy (−13.6 eV).
_explanation: The electron in the lowest level has an energy of −13.6 eV relative to being free. Supplying 13.6 eV raises it to zero energy (unbound), ionizing the atom, so this value measures how tightly the ground-state electron is held.

subject: physics
question_text: When white light passes through cool hydrogen gas, the spectrum shows dark lines at exactly the same positions where hot hydrogen gas shows bright emission lines. Why do the dark absorption lines match the bright emission lines?
_concept: correspondence of absorption and emission lines
_answer: Atoms absorb only photons whose energy matches an allowed transition between their levels — the same energy differences that produce emission — so absorption removes exactly those wavelengths, creating dark lines at the emission-line positions.
_explanation: The energy levels of an atom fix a set of allowed transition energies. In emission the atom releases photons of those energies; in absorption it takes up photons of the identical energies to jump up. Because both processes use the same level differences, the dark absorption lines coincide with the bright emission lines.

subject: physics
question_text: You can never predict when a single radioactive atom will decay, yet a large sample of the same atoms decays with a precise, reliable half-life. How can something completely random for one atom be perfectly predictable for many?
_concept: randomness of decay and statistical half-life
_answer: Radioactive decay is random with a fixed probability per atom per unit time; for a huge number of atoms these random events average out statistically, so a definite fraction (one half) decays each half-life.
_explanation: Each nucleus has a constant decay probability but no memory or schedule, so individual timing is unpredictable. Over an enormous population, the law of large numbers makes the fraction decaying in a given time essentially constant, producing the sharp, reproducible half-life.

subject: physics
question_text: In beta-minus decay a nucleus emits an electron, yet a nucleus contains only protons and neutrons — no electrons. Where does the emitted electron come from?
_answer: It is created at the moment of decay when a neutron transforms into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino; the electron is not a pre-existing orbital electron but is produced in the nuclear transformation.
_explanation: Beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton inside the nucleus, and to conserve charge and other quantities an electron (and an antineutrino) is created and ejected. So the electron originates from the neutron's transformation, not from the atom's electron cloud.

subject: physics
question_text: Small nuclei like helium have roughly equal numbers of protons and neutrons, but heavy nuclei like uranium contain far more neutrons than protons. Why do big nuclei need extra neutrons to stay together?
_answer: Protons repel each other electrically, and this repulsion grows with nuclear size, so heavy nuclei need extra neutrons — which add attractive strong-force binding without adding repulsion — to remain stable.
_explanation: The strong nuclear force binds all nucleons but acts only over a very short range, while the electrical repulsion between protons is long-range and builds up in large nuclei. Extra neutrons supply additional strong-force 'glue' without contributing to the repulsion, so the neutron-to-proton ratio rises for heavy, stable nuclei.

subject: physics
question_text: Adding pentavalent atoms creates an n-type semiconductor full of extra free electrons, and adding trivalent atoms creates a p-type full of holes — yet both materials are electrically neutral overall. How can a material full of extra electrons still be neutral?
_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
_answer: Each dopant atom is itself neutral (its protons match its electrons), so although it contributes a mobile carrier, the total positive and negative charge stay balanced; doping changes carrier type, not net charge.
_explanation: A dopant atom brings its own equal number of protons and electrons, so introducing it adds no net charge. In n-type material the extra mobile electrons are balanced by the fixed positive donor ions left behind, keeping the whole crystal electrically neutral despite the abundance of free carriers.

subject: physics
question_text: Right at the junction of a p-n diode there is a thin 'depletion region' with almost no free charge carriers, even though the p-side and n-side on either side are full of them. Why is this middle zone swept clean of carriers?
_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
_answer: Near the junction, electrons from the n-side and holes from the p-side diffuse across and recombine, leaving behind fixed ionized dopant atoms; the resulting built-in field pushes remaining mobile carriers away, so the region is depleted.
_explanation: Diffusion drives electrons and holes across the junction where they recombine, uncovering fixed charged donor and acceptor ions. These ions set up an electric field that repels further mobile carriers from the region, maintaining a carrier-free depletion layer with a built-in potential barrier.

subject: physics
question_text: A phone charger uses a diode to turn the alternating current from the wall socket into the direct current the phone needs. How does a one-way device turn AC into DC?
_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
_answer: A diode conducts only when forward biased, so it passes current during the half-cycles of one polarity and blocks the other, producing a pulsating one-directional (DC) output — the process of rectification.
_explanation: Because a diode allows current in only one direction, connecting it to AC lets only the favourable half-cycles through. A single diode gives half-wave rectification, while an arrangement of four diodes in a bridge rectifies both halves, converting alternating current into direct current.

subject: physics
question_text: Physicists describe current in a p-type semiconductor as carried by positively charged 'holes' moving through the crystal, even though the only real moving particles are negatively charged electrons. What exactly is a 'hole', and why treat it as a positive particle?
_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
_answer: A hole is a vacancy where an electron is missing from the bonding structure; as neighbouring electrons shift to fill it, the vacancy appears to move the other way, behaving like a positive charge carrier — a convenient description of collective electron motion.
_explanation: When an electron leaves a bond it creates an empty state, and successive electrons hopping into that vacancy make the empty spot migrate in the opposite direction. Tracking this moving absence is far simpler than tracking many individual electrons, so it is modelled as a positively charged particle called a hole.

subject: physics
question_text: A digital scale consistently reads 2.512 kg for an object every single time you weigh it, yet the object's true mass is 2.0 kg. Physicists would call this scale precise but not accurate. What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
_answer: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; precision is how closely repeated measurements agree with one another; a reading can be precise (consistent) yet inaccurate (consistently wrong), as with a miscalibrated scale.
_explanation: Accuracy concerns closeness to the true value, while precision concerns reproducibility and fineness of reading. A miscalibrated instrument gives tightly clustered but wrong readings — highly precise but inaccurate — showing the two qualities are independent.

subject: physics
question_text: Astronomers find the distance to a nearby star by watching how its apparent position shifts against far-off background stars as Earth moves from one side of its orbit to the other. How does this apparent shift reveal the star's distance?
_answer: The parallax method — the star's tiny angular shift seen from the two ends of Earth's orbit, combined with the known orbital baseline, gives the distance by trigonometry: distance ≈ baseline ÷ parallax angle (in radians).
_explanation: A nearby object appears to shift more against a distant background when viewed from two separated positions. Measuring the star's angular shift over Earth's orbital baseline and using the small-angle relation gives its distance, and the smaller the parallax the farther the star.

subject: physics
question_text: Throw a ball straight up and it takes exactly the same time to rise to its highest point as it does to fall back down to the level it was thrown from. Why are the rise time and the fall time equal?
_answer: Gravity gives the same constant acceleration throughout; the ball decelerates on the way up and accelerates symmetrically on the way down, returning to the launch level with the same speed, so the up and down times are equal.
_explanation: With constant gravitational acceleration and no air resistance, the motion is symmetric about the highest point. The ball loses speed going up at exactly the rate it gains speed coming down, so each half takes equal time and it returns with its original speed.

subject: physics
question_text: A stone dropped from rest gains about 9.8 m/s of speed during the first second of its fall, and again about 9.8 m/s during the second second, and so on. Why does it gain the same amount of speed every second rather than an increasing amount?
_concept: constant acceleration means uniform velocity gain
_answer: Because free-fall acceleration g is essentially constant; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so a constant g means the velocity increases by the same amount each second, even though the distance covered per second keeps growing.
_explanation: Constant acceleration means velocity changes at a steady rate. Gravity provides a nearly constant g near Earth's surface, so each second adds the same increment of speed; the distance per second grows only because the stone is already moving faster.

subject: physics
question_text: From the same height, one ball is simply dropped and another is thrown horizontally at the very same instant. Astonishingly, both strike the ground at exactly the same moment. Why doesn't the thrown ball, which travels much farther, take longer to land?
_concept: independence of horizontal and vertical motion
_answer: The horizontal and vertical motions are independent; the vertical fall depends only on gravity and the drop height, which are identical for both balls, so both take the same time to reach the ground regardless of horizontal motion.
_explanation: Projectile motion separates into independent horizontal and vertical components. The horizontal velocity has no effect on the vertical fall, which is governed only by gravity and the height. Since those are the same for both, they land together — the horizontal throw merely carries one ball farther sideways.

subject: physics
question_text: Once a projectile leaves your hand, its horizontal velocity stays constant for the whole flight (ignoring air resistance), even while its vertical velocity keeps changing. Why doesn't the horizontal speed slow down?
_concept: constant horizontal velocity in projectile motion
_answer: There is no horizontal force acting during the flight (gravity acts only vertically), so by Newton's first law the horizontal velocity is unchanged; only the vertical motion is affected by gravity.
_explanation: After launch the only force is gravity, which points straight down. With no horizontal force there is no horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal velocity component remains constant throughout, while gravity steadily alters the vertical component.

subject: physics
question_text: It takes a noticeably bigger push to get a heavy box moving from rest than to keep it sliding once it's already moving. Why is starting the motion harder than maintaining it?
_answer: The maximum static friction is generally larger than the kinetic friction, so a greater force is needed to overcome static friction and start motion; once sliding, the smaller kinetic friction resists it.
_explanation: Static friction can rise to a higher limiting value than the kinetic friction acting during sliding. You must exceed that larger static maximum to break the box loose, after which the smaller kinetic friction takes over, so less force is needed to keep it moving.

subject: physics
question_text: A rocket in the vacuum of space, with no air or ground to push against, still accelerates forward. If there is nothing external to push on, what does the rocket push against to move?
_answer: It pushes against its own ejected exhaust gases; by conservation of momentum, expelling mass backward at high speed gives the rocket equal and opposite forward momentum — no external medium is needed.
_explanation: Propulsion comes from Newton's third law and momentum conservation, not from pushing on air. The rocket throws exhaust backward, and the reaction to ejecting that momentum drives the rocket forward, which is exactly why rockets work perfectly in a vacuum.

subject: physics
question_text: When two lumps of clay collide head-on and stick together, momentum is conserved but a large amount of kinetic energy simply vanishes. Where does the missing kinetic energy go?
_concept: kinetic energy loss in inelastic collisions
_answer: Into other forms — heat, sound, and the work of permanently deforming the clay; momentum is always conserved, but in an inelastic collision kinetic energy is converted to these non-mechanical forms.
_explanation: Collisions always conserve momentum, but kinetic energy is conserved only in perfectly elastic ones. In a sticky, inelastic collision much of the kinetic energy is transformed into heat, sound, and deformation, so the final kinetic energy is less than the initial.

subject: physics
question_text: In a head-on elastic collision between two identical objects, the moving one stops dead while the stationary one moves off with the first one's exact original velocity — they simply exchange velocities. Why does this precise swap happen for equal masses?
_concept: velocity exchange in equal-mass elastic collisions
_answer: For equal masses in a one-dimensional elastic collision, conserving both momentum and kinetic energy forces the two objects to exchange velocities; the incoming object stops and the target moves off at the incoming speed.
_explanation: Solving the conservation equations for momentum and kinetic energy with equal masses gives a velocity swap as the only physical solution. This is why a moving billiard ball striking an identical stationary one head-on stops dead while the struck ball rolls away at the original speed.

subject: physics
question_text: Tightrope walkers usually carry a long, drooping pole across their bodies. How does holding this pole help them keep their balance?
_chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
_concept: increasing moment of inertia for stability
_answer: The long pole greatly increases the walker's moment of inertia, so any tipping (angular acceleration) is slowed for a given torque, giving more time to react; a drooping pole also lowers the centre of mass.
_explanation: A larger moment of inertia resists changes in rotational motion, so the walker topples far more slowly and can correct before losing balance. The pole's length places mass far from the body's axis to maximize this effect, and its downward droop lowers the combined centre of gravity for extra stability.

subject: physics
question_text: The very same rigid rod has a much larger moment of inertia when spun about an axis through one end than about an axis through its centre. Why does merely changing the axis change how hard the identical object is to rotate?
_chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
_concept: moment of inertia depends on the axis
_answer: Moment of inertia depends on how mass is distributed relative to the chosen axis (the sum of mr²); rotating about an end places more mass far from the axis than rotating about the centre, so the rod resists that rotation more.
_explanation: Unlike mass, moment of inertia is not a fixed property of the object alone — it depends on the axis. Mass farther from the axis contributes more (as r²), so an end axis, with mass spread out to the far end, gives a larger moment of inertia than a central axis for the same rod.

subject: physics
question_text: The acceleration due to gravity is slightly smaller at the equator than at the poles, so you weigh a little less at the equator. What is the main reason for this difference?
_concept: variation of effective g due to Earth's rotation
_answer: Earth's rotation — at the equator some of gravity must provide the centripetal force for the daily spin, reducing the effective g; Earth's equatorial bulge, placing the surface farther from the centre, adds to the effect.
_explanation: A point on the equator moves in a large circle as Earth rotates, so part of gravity is spent supplying the centripetal force, leaving a smaller effective weight. The poles lie on the rotation axis with no such motion, so effective g is greatest there, and Earth's slightly flattened shape reinforces the difference.

subject: physics
question_text: Two wires of the same material and thickness hang from a ceiling, but one is twice as long as the other. Under the same hanging load, the longer wire stretches twice as much. Why does length affect the stretch if the material and thickness are identical?
_concept: extension is proportional to original length
_answer: Extension equals (force × length) ÷ (area × Young's modulus), so for the same force, area, and modulus the extension is proportional to the original length; a longer wire accumulates the same fractional strain over a greater length.
_explanation: Young's modulus fixes the fractional stretch (strain) for a given stress, and strain is extension divided by original length. The same stress produces the same strain, but over a greater length that strain yields a larger absolute extension, so the longer wire stretches more.

subject: physics
question_text: Stretch a metal wire a little and it springs back to its original length, but stretch it too far and it stays permanently longer even after you let go. What has been exceeded when the wire no longer returns to its original length?
