question_text: A beam of light passing through a colloidal mixture like fog or dilute milk becomes visible as a bright path, but the same beam is invisible passing through a true solution like salt water. Why does the beam show up in one but not the other?
_answer: The Tyndall effect — colloidal particles are large enough to scatter light, making the beam's path visible, whereas the ions or molecules in a true solution are far too small to scatter light appreciably.
_explanation: Colloidal particles are of a size comparable to the wavelength of light, so they scatter it and reveal the beam's track. In a true solution the dissolved particles are much smaller and let light pass without noticeable scattering, so no visible path appears — a simple way to distinguish colloids from true solutions.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Gold and silver are often found in nature as the free metal, but reactive metals like sodium and aluminium are always found locked up in ores as compounds. Why does a metal's reactivity determine how it occurs in nature?
_chapter: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
_answer: Reactive metals readily combine with oxygen and other elements to form stable compounds, so they are found as ores; unreactive (noble) metals resist combining and therefore survive in nature as the free element.
_explanation: A metal's chemical activity decides whether it stays uncombined. Highly reactive metals long ago reacted with their surroundings to form stable minerals, so we find them as ores, while noble metals like gold, being inert, remain in metallic form even after millions of years.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Iron is extracted from its ore cheaply by heating with carbon, but aluminium cannot be obtained this way and instead requires costly electrolysis. Why can't the same carbon reduction be used to extract aluminium?
_chapter: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
_answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon and holds its oxygen very strongly, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide; the more powerful electrolytic reduction is needed to free aluminium from its ore.
_explanation: Carbon can only reduce the oxides of metals less reactive than itself, like iron. Aluminium's greater affinity for oxygen means carbon cannot strip the oxygen away, so electrolysis, which supplies electrons directly, is required to reduce aluminium oxide to the metal.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Nitrogen gas makes up most of the air we breathe and is so unreactive that it passes through our lungs harmlessly, yet nitrogen compounds such as TNT are explosively reactive. Why is molecular nitrogen (N₂) itself so inert?
_concept: inertness of nitrogen due to triple bond
_answer: N₂ has a very strong nitrogen-nitrogen triple bond with a high bond dissociation energy, so a great deal of energy is needed to break it apart, making molecular nitrogen extremely stable and unreactive.
_explanation: The three bonds holding the two nitrogen atoms together are exceptionally strong, so N₂ resists reacting under ordinary conditions. Only high-energy processes can break this triple bond; once nitrogen is combined into compounds, those bonds can release large amounts of energy, which is why nitrogen compounds can be so reactive.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Nitrogen can form NCl₃ but is unable to form NCl₅, whereas phosphorus, just below it in the same group, readily forms PCl₅. Why can phosphorus expand its bonding capacity but nitrogen cannot?
_concept: octet expansion and availability of d-orbitals
_answer: Nitrogen is in period 2 and has no accessible d-orbitals, so it can hold only eight electrons and form at most a limited number of bonds; phosphorus, in period 3, has available d-orbitals and can expand its octet to form five bonds as in PCl₅.
_explanation: Second-period elements like nitrogen are limited to the s and p orbitals of their shell, capping them at an octet. Phosphorus can use its empty 3d orbitals to accommodate more than eight electrons, allowing it to bond to five chlorines, something nitrogen physically cannot do.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Fluorine is the most electronegative element of all, yet it shows only the −1 oxidation state and never any positive oxidation state, unlike the other halogens which do. Why is fluorine restricted to −1?
_answer: Because fluorine is the most electronegative element and has no available d-orbitals, it can only gain or share electrons to reach −1; it is never less electronegative than its bonding partner, so it can never take a positive oxidation state.
_explanation: Positive oxidation states require an atom to give up electron density to a more electronegative partner, but nothing is more electronegative than fluorine. Lacking d-orbitals as well, fluorine cannot expand its bonding, so it is confined to the −1 state, unlike heavier halogens that can be positive.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Noble gases were long believed to form no compounds at all, but xenon does form compounds such as XeF₂, while helium and neon still form essentially none. Why can the heavier noble gases react while the lighter ones can't?
_answer: Heavier noble gases like xenon have larger atoms whose outer electrons are more loosely held (lower ionization energy), so highly electronegative elements such as fluorine and oxygen can bond with them; helium and neon hold their electrons too tightly to react.
_explanation: Reactivity requires an atom's electrons to be accessible for bonding. In the large xenon atom the outermost electrons are far from the nucleus and less tightly bound, allowing very electronegative partners to form bonds, whereas the small helium and neon atoms clutch their electrons so firmly that they remain effectively inert.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Compounds of transition metals are often vividly coloured — copper sulfate blue, potassium permanganate purple — whereas compounds of sodium or calcium are usually white. Why are so many transition metal compounds coloured?
_answer: In a transition metal ion the d-orbitals split into slightly different energy levels in the presence of surrounding ligands; electrons absorb specific visible wavelengths jumping between these split d-levels (d-d transitions), and the complementary colour is seen.
_explanation: The partly filled d-orbitals of transition metals split under the influence of ligands, and the gap between them happens to match visible-light energies. Absorbing part of the visible spectrum for these d-d transitions leaves the transmitted light coloured, which is why such compounds appear coloured while ions with no d-d transitions look white.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Transition metals commonly show several different oxidation states — iron can be +2 or +3, and manganese ranges from +2 up to +7 — whereas sodium is essentially always +1. Why do transition metals have so many oxidation states?
_concept: variable oxidation states of transition metals
_answer: The energies of the (n-1)d and the ns electrons are very close, so varying numbers of these electrons can be removed with comparable ease, giving rise to several stable oxidation states.
_explanation: In transition metals the outer d and s electrons lie at similar energies, so the metal can lose different numbers of them without a large energy penalty. This flexibility produces multiple oxidation states, unlike sodium, whose single valence electron gives essentially only the +1 state.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Transition metals and their compounds are used as catalysts in a huge range of industrial processes, from iron in ammonia manufacture to platinum in car exhaust converters. What property makes transition metals such effective catalysts?
_answer: Their variable oxidation states and their ability to form intermediate complexes (adsorbing and activating reactant molecules) let transition metals offer low-energy reaction pathways, speeding reactions up.
_explanation: Transition metals can readily change oxidation state and bind reactants on their surfaces or as complexes, providing an easier route for the reaction. By temporarily holding and activating the reacting molecules and then releasing the products, they lower the activation energy and are regenerated, acting as efficient catalysts.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature, while other transition metals are all solid. Why is mercury a liquid when its neighbours are solids?
_answer: Mercury's stable, filled electron configuration makes it hold its outer electrons tightly and share them poorly for metallic bonding, so the bonds between mercury atoms are unusually weak, giving it a very low melting point and keeping it liquid.
_explanation: Metallic bonding relies on atoms contributing electrons to a shared 'sea'. Mercury's electrons are held so tightly that they participate weakly in this bonding, so the interatomic forces are feeble. The resulting low melting point leaves mercury liquid at room temperature, unlike other transition metals with stronger metallic bonds.

subject: chemistry
question_text: In a coordination compound, a metal ion bonds to molecules like ammonia or water that are already electrically neutral and have all their own bonds satisfied. How can such a 'complete' neutral molecule form a bond to the metal?
_answer: The ligand donates a lone pair of electrons into an empty orbital on the metal ion, forming a coordinate (dative) bond in which both shared electrons originate from the ligand.
_explanation: Molecules like ammonia and water carry lone pairs of electrons not used in their own bonding. A metal ion with vacant orbitals accepts such a lone pair, and this donation forms a coordinate bond, allowing neutral molecules to attach to the metal even though they have no unpaired electrons to share.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Two coordination compounds can share the exact same overall formula yet have different colours and properties, differing only in whether a particular group is bonded to the metal or sits outside as a free counter-ion. What kind of isomerism is this?
_answer: It is ionization (or coordination-sphere) isomerism — the same atoms are distributed differently between the metal's coordination sphere and the ions outside it, producing distinct compounds with different properties.
_explanation: In these isomers a group may be directly bonded to the central metal in one compound but exist as a separate counter-ion in the other. Although the formulas match, this difference in what is inside versus outside the coordination sphere changes the compound's behaviour, such as which ions it releases in solution and its colour.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Haemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood by binding it to an iron centre, and carbon monoxide is deadly because it binds that very same iron. In terms of coordination chemistry, why is carbon monoxide so poisonous?
_answer: Carbon monoxide binds the iron in haemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen does, occupying the oxygen-binding site and blocking it, so haemoglobin can no longer pick up and transport oxygen.
_explanation: Both O₂ and CO act as ligands to the iron in haemoglobin, but CO's affinity is far greater. Once CO attaches, it holds on tightly and prevents oxygen from binding, so oxygen transport fails, which is why even small amounts of carbon monoxide are dangerous.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Adding excess ammonia to a pale blue copper sulfate solution turns it a deep, intense blue. In terms of coordination chemistry, what has changed around the copper ion?
_answer: Ammonia molecules replace the water ligands around the copper ion, forming the deep-blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion, whose different ligand field causes it to absorb light differently and appear a more intense blue.
_explanation: The copper ion is initially surrounded by water ligands, giving a pale blue. When stronger ammonia ligands displace the water, the new complex has a different d-orbital splitting, so it absorbs different wavelengths of light and shows a much deeper blue colour — a clear sign that ligand exchange has occurred.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Haloalkanes readily undergo reactions in which the halogen is replaced, but haloarenes (a halogen attached to a benzene ring) are far more resistant to the same kind of substitution. Why is the carbon-halogen bond in haloarenes so much harder to break?
_concept: unreactivity of the C–X bond in haloarenes
_answer: In haloarenes the carbon-halogen bond gains partial double-bond character through resonance with the ring and is attached to a less accessible sp² carbon, both of which strengthen the bond and hinder its replacement.
_explanation: The halogen's lone pairs delocalize into the aromatic ring, giving the C–X bond extra double-bond character that makes it stronger and shorter. Combined with the sp² carbon being harder for nucleophiles to approach, this makes substitution on haloarenes far more difficult than on haloalkanes.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A tertiary haloalkane undergoes one substitution mechanism (SN1) much faster than a primary one, but for the other mechanism (SN2) the order is exactly reversed. Why do the two substitution mechanisms favour opposite types of substrate?
_answer: SN1 proceeds through a carbocation, and tertiary carbocations are the most stable, so tertiary reacts fastest; SN2 requires an unhindered backside attack, which bulky groups block, so primary (least hindered) reacts fastest — hence the reversed trends.
_explanation: The two mechanisms have different rate-controlling factors. SN1's speed depends on how stable the carbocation intermediate is, favouring the highly substituted tertiary substrate. SN2's speed depends on the nucleophile reaching the carbon from behind, which crowding by alkyl groups prevents, so it favours the open primary substrate.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are so chemically stable that they are harmless where we use them at ground level, yet they cause serious damage to the ozone layer high in the atmosphere. How can such unreactive compounds end up being so harmful?
_answer: Their very stability lets CFCs survive long enough to drift intact into the stratosphere, where intense ultraviolet light breaks them apart to release chlorine radicals that catalytically destroy large numbers of ozone molecules.
_explanation: Because CFCs do not react at lower altitudes, they persist and rise to the stratosphere. There, high-energy UV radiation splits them, freeing chlorine atoms that act as catalysts, each destroying many ozone molecules before being regenerated, so their inertness at ground level is exactly what allows them to reach and harm the ozone layer.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Ethanol (an alcohol) boils at a much higher temperature than dimethyl ether, even though both have the identical molecular formula C₂H₆O. Why does the alcohol boil so much higher than the ether?
_answer: Ethanol has an O–H group that lets its molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, requiring extra energy to separate them for boiling; dimethyl ether has no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond and boils at a much lower temperature.
_explanation: Although the two compounds have the same atoms, only the alcohol has a hydrogen attached to oxygen, enabling strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Breaking these additional attractions requires more heat, so ethanol boils far higher than the ether, whose molecules are held together only by weaker forces.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Phenol is acidic enough to react with sodium hydroxide, but ordinary alcohols like ethanol are not, even though both contain an O–H group. Why is the O–H in phenol so much more acidic than the O–H in an alcohol?
_answer: When phenol loses its proton, the resulting phenoxide ion is stabilized by resonance that delocalizes the negative charge into the benzene ring, so phenol gives up H⁺ readily; the alkoxide from an alcohol has no such stabilization, so alcohols are far less acidic.
_explanation: Acidity depends on how stable the anion left behind is. The phenoxide ion spreads its negative charge over the aromatic ring through resonance, making it relatively stable and phenol relatively acidic. An alcohol's alkoxide ion localizes the charge on one oxygen with no resonance help, so it forms less easily and the alcohol is only very weakly acidic.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Small alcohols such as ethanol mix with water in all proportions, but larger alcohols like octanol barely dissolve at all. Why does increasing the carbon chain length reduce an alcohol's solubility in water?
_answer: The –OH group hydrogen-bonds with water and promotes solubility, but the nonpolar hydrocarbon chain is water-repelling; as the chain grows longer it increasingly dominates, so large alcohols become mostly insoluble.
_explanation: An alcohol's water solubility is a tug-of-war between its water-friendly –OH group and its water-hating carbon chain. In small alcohols the –OH wins and they mix freely, but in larger alcohols the long hydrophobic chain outweighs the single –OH, so solubility drops sharply with chain length.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Carboxylic acids are much more acidic than alcohols or even phenols, despite all three containing an O–H group. Why is the O–H of a carboxylic acid so much more acidic?
_answer: The carboxylate ion formed on losing the proton is strongly stabilized by resonance that spreads the negative charge equally over two oxygen atoms, so the acid parts with its H⁺ very readily, making it far more acidic than alcohols or phenols.
_explanation: After a carboxylic acid loses its proton, the resulting negative charge is shared symmetrically between two oxygens through resonance, giving an especially stable anion. This strong stabilization drives the acid to ionize much more than an alcohol or phenol, whose conjugate bases are less effectively stabilized.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Aldehydes generally undergo nucleophilic addition reactions faster than ketones do. Why is an aldehyde more reactive toward nucleophiles than a ketone?
_answer: A ketone has two electron-donating alkyl groups that reduce the positive character of the carbonyl carbon and crowd it sterically; an aldehyde has fewer, so its carbonyl carbon is more electrophilic and more accessible to nucleophiles, making it react faster.
_explanation: Nucleophilic addition attacks the electron-poor carbonyl carbon. Alkyl groups both push electron density onto that carbon (reducing its attraction for nucleophiles) and physically block approach. Since aldehydes carry at most one alkyl group versus a ketone's two, their carbonyl carbon is both more positive and less hindered, so it reacts more readily.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A carboxylic acid like acetic acid boils at a higher temperature than an alcohol of similar molecular weight, even though both can form hydrogen bonds. Why does the acid boil even higher?
_answer: Carboxylic acid molecules pair up into dimers held together by two hydrogen bonds, effectively doubling the size of the unit that must be separated, so more energy is needed to boil them than a comparable alcohol.
_explanation: While alcohols form single hydrogen bonds between molecules, carboxylic acids form two hydrogen bonds between pairs of molecules, locking them into stable dimers. Boiling requires breaking these double links and separating the larger effective units, so the acid's boiling point exceeds that of a similar-weight alcohol.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Amines act as bases in water, accepting a proton, even though they contain no hydroxide ions of their own. What makes an amine basic?
_answer: The nitrogen atom in an amine has a lone pair of electrons that it can donate to accept a proton (H⁺), forming an ammonium ion; this availability of a lone pair is what gives the amine its basic character.
_explanation: Basicity here means the ability to accept a proton, and the amine nitrogen's lone pair is well suited to bond to an incoming H⁺. By using this lone pair to grab a proton from water, the amine acts as a base and generates hydroxide ions in solution, even though it contains none to begin with.

subject: chemistry
question_text: In the gas phase, adding more alkyl groups steadily makes an amine a stronger base, but in water solution the order of basicity becomes irregular. Why does dissolving the amines in water scramble the trend?
_answer: In water, basicity depends not only on electron donation by alkyl groups but also on how well the protonated cation is stabilized by hydrogen bonding with water; bulky alkyl groups hinder this solvation, so the competing effects give an irregular order.
_explanation: Alkyl groups increase electron density on nitrogen (favouring basicity) but also crowd the resulting cation and block water molecules from stabilizing it by hydrogen bonding. In the gas phase only the first effect operates, giving a clean trend, but in water the two opposing effects combine to produce the observed irregular basicity order.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Aniline, in which an amino group is attached to a benzene ring, is a much weaker base than an aliphatic amine like methylamine. Why does attaching the amino group to a benzene ring reduce its basicity?
_answer: In aniline the nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring by resonance, making it less available to accept a proton, so aniline is a weaker base than an aliphatic amine whose lone pair is fully available.
_explanation: Basicity depends on how freely the nitrogen lone pair can bond to a proton. In aniline that lone pair is drawn into the benzene ring through resonance, so it is partly tied up and less able to grab a proton, whereas in methylamine the lone pair is entirely free, making it the stronger base.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Enzymes can accelerate biochemical reactions by factors of millions, but they work well only within narrow ranges of temperature and pH. Why are enzymes so sensitive to their conditions?
_answer: Enzymes are proteins whose precise three-dimensional shape, especially the active site, is essential for their catalytic function; extremes of temperature or pH disrupt this folded structure (denaturation), destroying their activity.
_explanation: An enzyme's ability to catalyse depends on the exact shape of its active site, which fits its target molecule. Heat or unfavourable pH breaks the weak interactions maintaining the fold, unravelling the protein and deforming the active site, so the enzyme loses its function outside its optimal conditions.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Glucose and fructose share the identical molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆, yet they taste different and are handled differently by the body. Why do two sugars with the same formula behave so differently?
_answer: They are isomers with different structural arrangements — glucose contains an aldehyde group (an aldose) while fructose contains a ketone group (a ketose) — so their different functional groups and shapes give them different properties.
_explanation: Having the same formula does not mean the same structure. Glucose and fructose arrange their atoms differently, with glucose carrying an aldehyde and fructose a ketone functional group. These structural differences change how the molecules taste and how enzymes recognize and process them, despite the identical formula.

subject: chemistry
question_text: The two strands of a DNA molecule are held together only by relatively weak hydrogen bonds, yet DNA is stable enough to safeguard genetic information for an entire lifetime. How can such weak individual bonds create so stable a structure?
_answer: Although each hydrogen bond between the base pairs is weak on its own, an enormous number of them run the length of the long complementary strands, and together they add up to great collective stability while still allowing the strands to be separated for copying.
_explanation: A single hydrogen bond is easily broken, but DNA contains millions of them along its paired strands. Their combined strength holds the double helix firmly together, giving the molecule its durability, yet because the bonds are individually weak, the strands can be unzipped locally when the genetic information needs to be read or replicated.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Natural rubber is soft and turns sticky when warm, but after being treated with sulfur in a process called vulcanization it becomes strong and springy. What does sulfur do to rubber at the molecular level?
_answer: Sulfur forms cross-links (bridges) between the long rubber polymer chains, tying them together so they can no longer slide freely past one another, which gives the rubber its strength and elasticity.
_explanation: In raw rubber the polymer chains can slip, making it soft and prone to becoming sticky when heated. Vulcanization introduces sulfur bridges that link the chains at intervals, forming a network that resists deformation and springs back, so the treated rubber is tougher, more elastic, and less temperature-sensitive.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Some plastics soften and can be remoulded when heated (thermoplastics), while others set permanently and char rather than melt when strongly heated (thermosetting plastics). Why do these two kinds of plastic behave so differently on heating?
_answer: Thermoplastics consist of separate polymer chains held together by weak forces that loosen on heating, so they soften and can be remoulded; thermosetting plastics have extensive covalent cross-links forming a rigid three-dimensional network that cannot be remelted.
_explanation: The difference lies in the bonding between chains. In thermoplastics the chains are held by weak intermolecular forces that give way when heated, allowing repeated softening and shaping. Thermosets are locked by strong covalent cross-links into a permanent network, so heating cannot loosen them and they decompose rather than melt.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Soap can wash away greasy dirt even though grease does not dissolve in water at all. How does a soap molecule bridge the gap between water and oily grease?
_concept: cleansing action of soap and micelles
_answer: A soap molecule has a water-loving (hydrophilic) head and an oil-loving (hydrophobic) tail; the tails embed in the grease while the heads face the water, forming micelles that lift the grease off and carry it away in the water.
_explanation: Soap works because its two ends have opposite affinities. The hydrophobic tails dissolve into grease and the hydrophilic heads point outward into the water, so grease becomes wrapped in tiny droplets called micelles. These are suspended in the water and rinsed away, allowing soap to remove dirt that water alone cannot.

subject: chemistry
question_text: An antacid tablet relieves the discomfort of an acidic stomach, but taking too much can upset the stomach's normal function. In simple chemical terms, how does an antacid work?
_answer: Antacids are mild bases that neutralize the excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach through an acid-base reaction, raising the pH and relieving the discomfort caused by too much acid.
_explanation: The stomach uses hydrochloric acid for digestion, and excess acid causes discomfort. An antacid, being a mild base such as a metal hydroxide or carbonate, reacts with and neutralizes some of this acid, lowering the acidity. Overuse, however, can neutralize too much acid and interfere with normal digestion.

subject: chemistry
question_text: When a candle burns down to almost nothing, it looks as though its mass has simply vanished into thin air. Yet chemists insist mass is conserved. Where did the candle's mass actually go?
_answer: It was converted into gases — carbon dioxide and water vapour — that escaped into the air; if you weighed the candle plus the oxygen consumed against the gases produced, the total mass is unchanged.
_explanation: Burning doesn't destroy matter; it rearranges atoms into new substances. The wax combines with oxygen to form CO₂ and water vapour that drift away invisibly, so the mass only seems to disappear. Accounting for the oxygen used and the gases released shows mass is conserved.

subject: chemistry
question_text: The molarity of a solution changes slightly when you warm or cool it, but its molality stays exactly the same at every temperature. Why does one concentration measure shift with temperature while the other doesn't?
_answer: Molarity is defined per litre of solution, and volume expands or contracts with temperature, so it changes; molality is defined per kilogram of solvent, and mass is unaffected by temperature, so it stays constant.
_explanation: Because molarity uses volume, which is temperature-dependent, heating a solution changes its molarity even though no solute is added or removed. Molality relies on the mass of solvent, which never changes with temperature, making molality the temperature-independent measure of concentration.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A metal forms two different oxides, and the masses of oxygen combining with a fixed mass of the metal are always in a simple whole-number ratio, such as 1 to 2. Which law of chemical combination does this illustrate?
_answer: The law of multiple proportions — when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in small whole-number ratios.
_explanation: This regularity reflects that atoms combine in fixed, whole-number ratios. Since the metal can bond with different whole numbers of oxygen atoms in its two oxides, the oxygen masses per fixed mass of metal fall into a simple ratio, exactly as the law of multiple proportions predicts.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Two atoms of the same element can have noticeably different masses, yet they behave identically in every chemical reaction. How can atoms differ in mass but not in chemistry?
_answer: They are isotopes — atoms with the same number of protons and electrons (which determine chemical behaviour) but different numbers of neutrons, which change only the mass.
_explanation: Chemistry is governed by the electrons, and the number of electrons matches the number of protons, which is identical for isotopes of an element. Extra or fewer neutrons alter the mass but not the electron arrangement, so isotopes react the same way while weighing differently.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Chromium's electron configuration is 3d⁵ 4s¹ rather than the expected 3d⁴ 4s², as if it 'promotes' one 4s electron into the 3d subshell. Why does chromium rearrange its electrons this way?
_concept: stability of half-filled and fully-filled subshells
_answer: A half-filled 3d⁵ (together with a half-filled 4s¹) configuration is extra stable due to symmetry and exchange energy, so chromium adopts it in preference to 3d⁴ 4s².
_explanation: Exactly half-filled and fully-filled subshells have lowered energy from favourable electron exchange and symmetrical charge distribution. This extra stability is enough for chromium to shift one electron from 4s to 3d, giving the unexpected but lower-energy 3d⁵ 4s¹ arrangement (a similar effect occurs for copper).

subject: chemistry
question_text: Any single orbital in an atom can hold at most two electrons, and never three or more. Why is an orbital strictly limited to two electrons?
_answer: The Pauli exclusion principle forbids two electrons from having identical sets of quantum numbers; an orbital's three quantum numbers are fixed, so only the two possible opposite spins remain, capping it at two electrons.
_explanation: Each electron is described by four quantum numbers, and no two electrons in an atom can share all four. Since an orbital fixes the first three, the only freedom left is the spin, which has just two values, so an orbital can accommodate exactly two electrons of opposite spin.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Every electron in an atom is described by a unique set of four 'quantum numbers'. Why do we need as many as four numbers to pin down a single electron?
_answer: Three quantum numbers (n, l, m) specify the orbital's size, shape, and orientation, and a fourth (spin) distinguishes the two electrons that can share that orbital, so together they uniquely identify each electron.
_explanation: An electron's state requires specifying which shell (n), the subshell shape (l), the spatial orientation (m), and its spin. These four numbers together give every electron a unique 'address', which is why no two electrons in an atom can have the identical set.

subject: chemistry
question_text: The energy of an electron bound in a hydrogen atom is always written as a negative number. What does it mean for an electron to have negative energy?
_answer: The negative sign indicates the electron is bound to the nucleus, having lower energy than a free electron at rest (which is taken as zero); energy must be supplied to pull it away to infinity.
_explanation: Energy is measured relative to a free, motionless electron infinitely far from the nucleus, defined as zero. Because a bound electron is at lower energy than that reference, its energy is negative, and the deeper (more negative) it is, the more energy is needed to ionize the atom.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Moving down a group in the periodic table, atoms get larger even though each element has more protons pulling on the electrons. Why doesn't the increasing nuclear charge shrink the atoms as you go down?
_chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
_concept: atomic radius trend down a group
_answer: Each step down the group adds a whole new electron shell, and the increased distance plus greater shielding by inner electrons outweigh the rising nuclear charge, so the atoms get bigger.
_explanation: Down a group, electrons occupy successively higher shells farther from the nucleus, and the inner electrons shield the outer ones from the full nuclear pull. These effects dominate over the added protons, so atomic size increases despite the greater nuclear charge.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A sodium ion (Na⁺) is much smaller than a sodium atom, but a chloride ion (Cl⁻) is much larger than a chlorine atom. Why do a cation and an anion change size in opposite directions?
_chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
_concept: ionic radii of cations and anions
_answer: Losing an electron (forming the cation) removes an outer shell and increases the pull per remaining electron, shrinking it; gaining an electron (forming the anion) adds electron-electron repulsion in the same shell, expanding it.
_explanation: When sodium loses its lone outer electron, it also loses a whole shell and the remaining electrons are held more tightly, so the cation is smaller. When chlorine gains an electron, the extra electron increases repulsion within the outer shell and the same nuclear charge holds more electrons, so the anion swells.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Most elements release energy when they gain an electron, but the noble gases actually require energy to accept one. Why do noble gases resist taking on an extra electron?
_chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
_concept: electron gain enthalpy of noble gases
_answer: Noble gases have completely filled outer shells, so an added electron would have to enter a new, higher-energy shell; this is unfavourable, giving them positive electron gain enthalpy.
_explanation: An incoming electron is only released with energy if it can enter a stable, low-energy vacancy. Noble gases already have full shells, so the extra electron must go into the next shell far from the nucleus, which costs energy rather than releasing it — hence their positive electron gain enthalpy.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Across a period, elements change from shiny, conducting metals on the left to dull, non-conducting nonmetals on the right. What underlying trend drives this shift from metallic to non-metallic character?
_chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
_concept: metallic to non-metallic character across a period
_answer: Across a period the effective nuclear charge rises and atoms hold their electrons more tightly, so elements go from readily losing electrons (metallic) on the left to readily gaining them (non-metallic) on the right.
_explanation: Metallic character depends on how easily an element loses electrons. As nuclear charge increases across a period, ionization energy rises and electron affinity grows, so elements shift from giving up electrons (metals) toward attracting them (nonmetals), changing metallic character to non-metallic.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Solid table salt does not conduct electricity at all, yet molten salt or salt dissolved in water conducts readily. Why does the same compound switch from insulator to conductor?
_answer: In the solid, the ions are locked rigidly in the lattice and cannot move; melting or dissolving frees the ions to move around, and moving ions can carry electric charge, so the substance conducts.
_explanation: Electrical conduction requires mobile charge carriers. In solid salt the oppositely charged ions are fixed in position, so no charge flows, but once the lattice is broken down by melting or dissolving, the ions become free to migrate toward the electrodes and conduct current.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Water, hydrogen fluoride, and ammonia have surprisingly high boiling points compared with the heavier hydrides of their own groups, which should boil higher based on mass alone. What accounts for these anomalously high boiling points?
_answer: These molecules form strong hydrogen bonds, because hydrogen is attached to the highly electronegative atoms fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen; breaking these extra bonds requires much more energy, raising the boiling points.
_explanation: When H is bonded to F, O, or N, the large electronegativity difference creates strong dipoles that let molecules hydrogen-bond to one another. These bonds are much stronger than ordinary intermolecular forces, so HF, H₂O, and NH₃ boil far higher than expected from molecular mass alone.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A metal can be hammered flat into thin sheets or drawn into wire without shattering, whereas an ionic crystal cracks apart under the same blow. Why are metals malleable while ionic solids are brittle?
_answer: In a metal, positive ions sit in a mobile 'sea' of delocalized electrons, so layers can slide past one another without breaking the bonding; in an ionic solid, shifting layers brings like charges together, and the repulsion splits the crystal.
_explanation: Metallic bonding is non-directional, so displacing layers of metal ions leaves them still bound by the surrounding electron sea, allowing shaping without fracture. In ionic crystals, however, sliding a layer aligns like-charged ions whose repulsion cleaves the crystal, making it brittle.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Some compounds we call 'ionic', such as aluminium chloride, actually behave more like covalent substances. What makes an ionic bond take on covalent character?
_answer: A small, highly charged cation (like Al³⁺) has strong polarizing power and distorts the electron cloud of a large, easily polarized anion, pulling shared electron density between them — so the bond acquires covalent character (Fajans' rules).
_explanation: According to Fajans' rules, a cation that is small and highly charged tugs strongly on a nearby anion's electron cloud. If the anion is large and easily deformed, the electrons are drawn into the space between the ions rather than staying fully transferred, giving the 'ionic' bond significant covalent character.

subject: chemistry
question_text: In methane the four H–C–H bond angles are about 109.5°, not the 90° you might expect if carbon simply used its three mutually perpendicular p orbitals plus an s orbital. Why are the angles 109.5°?
_answer: Carbon's one s and three p orbitals mix to form four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals that point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving the characteristic 109.5° angles that maximize separation of the bonding pairs.
_explanation: Rather than using its atomic orbitals directly, carbon blends them into four identical sp³ hybrids arranged tetrahedrally. This geometry spreads the four bonding electron pairs as far apart as possible, producing the observed 109.5° angles instead of the 90° that unmixed p orbitals would give.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Hydrogen chloride is a covalent molecule, yet when it dissolves in water it produces hydrogen and chloride ions. How can a covalent compound break up into ions in water?
_concept: polar covalent bonds and ionization in water
_answer: The H–Cl bond is strongly polar, with partial positive and negative ends; polar water molecules surround and stabilize these partial charges, pulling the molecule apart into fully separated H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
_explanation: Although HCl shares electrons covalently, the sharing is very uneven, giving the bond a strong dipole. Water, being highly polar, solvates and stabilizes the resulting ions, providing enough energy to complete the separation of the already-polarized bond into free ions in solution.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Open a bottle of ammonia at one end of a long tube and a bottle of hydrogen chloride at the other; a white ring of ammonium chloride forms, but closer to the hydrogen chloride end. Why doesn't the ring form exactly in the middle?
_answer: By Graham's law, lighter gases diffuse faster; ammonia is lighter than hydrogen chloride, so it travels farther in the same time, and the two gases meet nearer the heavier hydrogen chloride end.
_explanation: The rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass. Ammonia, being lighter, moves faster than the heavier HCl, so in the time they take to meet, ammonia covers more of the tube, forming the white ring closer to the HCl source.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Small droplets of a liquid, like dew or mercury beads, naturally take on a spherical shape rather than any other form. What drives a free liquid drop to become a sphere?
_concept: surface tension and minimum surface area
_answer: Surface tension acts to minimize the liquid's surface area, and for a given volume a sphere has the smallest possible surface area, so free drops pull themselves into spheres.
_explanation: Molecules at a liquid's surface are pulled inward by their neighbours, creating surface tension that tends to shrink the surface. Since a sphere encloses a given volume with the least surface, the drop adopts a spherical shape to reach this lowest-energy state.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Honey and other liquids flow more easily when warmed, so heating lowers their viscosity; yet heating a gas actually increases its viscosity. Why do liquids and gases respond to heat in opposite ways?
_answer: In liquids, heating weakens the intermolecular attractions that resist flow, lowering viscosity; in gases, viscosity comes from momentum transfer between layers by moving molecules, and heating speeds them up, increasing that transfer and raising viscosity.
_explanation: Liquid viscosity arises from molecules sticking to their neighbours, so warming, which loosens these attractions, makes the liquid flow more freely. Gas viscosity instead comes from fast molecules carrying momentum between layers; higher temperature makes them move faster and exchange more momentum, so gas viscosity rises with heat.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A messy room never tidies itself, and heat never flows on its own from a cold object to a hot one. What single overarching principle governs the direction of both of these everyday observations?
_concept: second law of thermodynamics and entropy
_answer: The second law of thermodynamics — the total entropy (disorder) of the universe always increases in any spontaneous process, so events proceed toward greater overall disorder.
_explanation: Spontaneous changes are those that increase the entropy of the universe. Both a room becoming disordered and heat flowing from hot to cold represent increases in total entropy, whereas the reverse processes would decrease it, which the second law forbids without outside input.

subject: chemistry
question_text: The standard enthalpy of formation of oxygen gas (O₂) is defined as exactly zero, and the same is true for every element in its standard state. Why is an element's enthalpy of formation taken to be zero?
_concept: standard enthalpy of formation of elements
_answer: Enthalpy of formation measures the heat change when a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states; forming an element from itself involves no change, so by definition its standard enthalpy of formation is zero.
_explanation: The scale of formation enthalpies needs a reference point, and elements in their most stable standard form are chosen as that zero. Since 'making' an element out of the very same element requires no reaction and no enthalpy change, its standard enthalpy of formation is defined as zero.

subject: chemistry
question_text: You can raise a gas's temperature either by heating it or by compressing it (doing work on it) with no heat added at all. What does this reveal about the nature of internal energy?
_concept: first law and equivalence of heat and work
_answer: Internal energy can be increased by supplying heat or by doing work, and the gas cannot tell the difference; the first law (ΔU = q + w) treats heat and work as two interchangeable ways of adding energy.
_explanation: Internal energy depends only on the state of the gas, not on how energy was delivered. Whether energy enters as heat or as compression work, the internal energy (and temperature) rises the same way, illustrating that heat and work are equivalent means of changing a system's energy.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Breaking a chemical bond always requires an input of energy, while forming a bond always releases energy. Why are these two processes energetically opposite?
_answer: A bond is a stable, low-energy arrangement, so energy must be supplied to pull the atoms apart (endothermic), while letting atoms come together into a bond releases that energy (exothermic); a reaction's net energy is bonds broken minus bonds formed.
_explanation: Bonded atoms sit at lower energy than separated ones, so separating them costs energy and joining them gives energy back. Whether a reaction overall absorbs or releases heat depends on the balance between the energy needed to break the reactant bonds and the energy released in forming the product bonds.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Adding solid sodium acetate to a solution of acetic acid actually suppresses the acid's ionization, making it dissociate less. Why does adding a shared ion push the acid to ionize less?
_answer: The common ion effect — the added acetate ions increase the concentration of a product of the acid's dissociation equilibrium, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts back toward the un-ionized acid.
_explanation: Acetic acid's dissociation produces acetate ions, and adding more acetate from the salt raises that product's concentration. The equilibrium responds by shifting to consume the excess, driving the reaction back toward undissociated acid, so the acid ionizes less than it would alone.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Mixing two perfectly clear solutions can suddenly produce a cloudy solid that settles out. In terms of equilibrium, what condition triggers a precipitate to form?
_answer: A precipitate forms when the product of the relevant ion concentrations (the ionic product) exceeds the salt's solubility product (Ksp); the solution can no longer hold that many ions dissolved, so the excess separates as solid.
_explanation: Each sparingly soluble salt has a characteristic solubility product that its dissolved ions cannot exceed. When mixing solutions raises the ionic product above Ksp, the solution becomes supersaturated with respect to that salt, and the extra ions combine and precipitate to restore equilibrium.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Even the purest water conducts electricity very faintly and always has a pH of 7 at room temperature. What does this tiny conductivity reveal about water itself?
_answer: Water molecules slightly self-ionize into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions (autoionization, described by Kw); these small equal concentrations give pure water its faint conductivity and a pH of 7 at 25°C.
_explanation: A very small fraction of water molecules transfer a proton to one another, producing equal tiny amounts of hydrogen and hydroxide ions. These few ions allow slight conduction, and because their concentrations are equal, pure water is neutral with a pH of 7 at room temperature.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A solution of sodium carbonate turns out to be distinctly basic, even though it is simply a dissolved salt and contains no added base. Why is this salt solution not neutral?
_answer: Salt hydrolysis — the carbonate ion is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it reacts with water to grab protons and generate hydroxide ions, making the solution basic.
_explanation: When a salt of a strong base and a weak acid dissolves, its anion is basic enough to react with water. The carbonate ions take protons from water molecules, releasing OH⁻ ions and raising the pH, so the solution ends up basic rather than neutral.

subject: chemistry
question_text: In any redox reaction, the substance called the oxidizing agent is itself reduced during the reaction. Why does the 'oxidizer' end up gaining electrons?
_answer: An oxidizing agent works by taking electrons away from another substance (oxidizing it); accepting those electrons means the oxidizing agent is itself reduced.
_explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain. The oxidizing agent causes oxidation in its partner by pulling electrons off it, and since those electrons have to go somewhere, the oxidizing agent gains them and is therefore reduced — the two processes always accompany each other.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A clean copper wire dipped into silver nitrate solution slowly becomes coated with glittering silver, while the solution turns blue. Why does copper displace silver from the solution?
_answer: Copper is more reactive (more easily oxidized) than silver, so copper atoms give up electrons to the silver ions; the silver ions are reduced to metallic silver on the wire while copper enters solution as blue Cu²⁺ ions.
_explanation: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive one from its salt. Copper, being above silver in the reactivity series, readily loses electrons to Ag⁺ ions, reducing them to silver metal that coats the wire, and the dissolved copper(II) ions give the solution its blue colour.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Iron is often coated with a layer of zinc (galvanizing) to stop it rusting, and remarkably the iron stays protected even if the zinc layer gets scratched and the iron is exposed. Why does zinc protect iron even where the iron is bare?
_answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it acts as a sacrificial anode — it oxidizes (corrodes) in preference to the iron, giving up its electrons to protect the iron cathodically even at scratched, exposed spots.
_explanation: Because zinc loses electrons more readily than iron, it corrodes first, supplying electrons that keep the iron from oxidizing. This sacrificial protection continues as long as zinc remains, so a scratch that bares the iron doesn't cause rusting until the surrounding zinc is used up.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Ordinary water and so-called 'heavy water' look and taste alike, yet heavy water is harmful to most living things if it replaces normal water in the body. What is chemically different about heavy water?
_answer: Heavy water (D₂O) contains deuterium — an isotope of hydrogen carrying an extra neutron — in place of ordinary hydrogen; the heavier atoms slow down biochemical reactions enough to disrupt normal cellular processes.
_explanation: Deuterium behaves chemically like hydrogen but weighs about twice as much, so bonds involving it break more slowly. When heavy water widely replaces normal water in an organism, these slowed reaction rates interfere with the finely tuned biochemistry of cells, making heavy water toxic in large amounts.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Hydrogen is promoted as a clean fuel because burning it produces only water and no carbon dioxide. Why is hydrogen considered pollution-free at the point where it is burned?
_answer: When hydrogen burns it combines with oxygen to form only water vapour, releasing no carbon dioxide or other carbon-based pollutants, so its combustion itself is clean.
_explanation: Because hydrogen contains no carbon, its only combustion product is water, unlike fossil fuels that release CO₂ and other pollutants. This makes burning hydrogen pollution-free at the point of use, although how cleanly the hydrogen is produced is a separate consideration.

subject: chemistry
question_text: The Group 2 metals such as calcium are noticeably less reactive than the Group 1 metals right beside them, such as potassium. Why does having two valence electrons make a metal less reactive, not more?
_answer: Group 2 metals must lose two electrons and have a smaller size and higher nuclear charge than their Group 1 neighbours, so their higher ionization energies make them hold onto electrons more tightly and react less readily.
_explanation: Reactivity of these metals depends on how easily electrons are lost. Group 2 atoms are smaller with a greater nuclear pull and must surrender two electrons rather than one, so their higher ionization energy makes them less eager to react than the larger, single-electron Group 1 metals.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Alkali metals such as sodium and potassium are so soft they can be sliced with an ordinary knife, unlike hard metals such as iron. Why are the alkali metals so soft?
_concept: weak metallic bonding in alkali metals
_answer: Alkali metals have only one valence electron per atom and relatively large atoms, so the metallic bonding holding the atoms together is weak, making the metals soft and easy to cut.
_explanation: The strength of a metal depends on how many electrons each atom contributes to the shared electron sea and how closely packed the ions are. With just one loosely held electron per large atom, alkali metals form weak metallic bonds, so the atoms are held together feebly and the metal is soft.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Calcium, strontium, and barium impart characteristic colours to a flame, but beryllium and magnesium, at the top of the same group, do not. Why do only the heavier Group 2 metals give flame colours?
_concept: flame colours and ionization energy in Group 2
_answer: Beryllium and magnesium are small with high ionization energies, so their electrons are held too tightly to be excited by a flame's energy; the larger atoms lower down hold their electrons more loosely, so a flame can excite them to emit colour.
_explanation: A flame colour requires electrons to be excited to higher levels and then emit light as they fall back. In the tiny beryllium and magnesium atoms the electrons are bound too strongly for a flame to excite them, whereas the bigger, lower-ionization-energy atoms of calcium, strontium, and barium are excited easily and glow with characteristic colours.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Diborane (B₂H₆) contains more bonds than it has pairs of electrons to make ordinary two-electron bonds. How can such an 'electron-deficient' molecule hold itself together?
_answer: Diborane uses three-centre two-electron 'bridge' (banana) bonds, in which a single pair of electrons is shared among three atoms (B–H–B), letting it bind together despite not having enough electrons for all-normal bonds.
_explanation: Because boron is electron-deficient, diborane cannot form conventional two-electron bonds everywhere. Instead, two bridging hydrogens each share one electron pair across two boron atoms, spreading electrons over three centres. These unusual bridge bonds hold the electron-deficient molecule together.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Silicon dioxide (quartz, sand) is a hard solid that melts only at very high temperatures, but carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature — even though both are dioxides of Group 14 elements. Why are they so different?
_concept: network versus molecular structures of Group 14 oxides
_answer: Silicon dioxide forms a giant covalent network in which every silicon is bonded to four oxygens throughout the crystal, requiring enormous energy to break; carbon dioxide forms small, discrete O=C=O molecules held together only by weak intermolecular forces, so it is a gas.
_explanation: Carbon readily forms strong pπ–pπ double bonds, giving discrete CO₂ molecules that separate easily. Silicon prefers single bonds and instead links to four oxygens in a continuous three-dimensional network, so melting SiO₂ means breaking a vast lattice of covalent bonds, making it a hard, high-melting solid.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Aluminium oxide reacts with acids and also reacts with bases. What is a substance that reacts with both acids and bases called, and why does alumina behave this way?
_answer: It is an amphoteric oxide — aluminium sits on the metal/nonmetal borderline, so its oxide can act as a base toward acids and as an acid toward bases, reacting with either.
_explanation: Amphoteric substances show both acidic and basic behaviour. Aluminium is neither strongly metallic nor strongly non-metallic, so its oxide can neutralize acids like a basic metal oxide and also dissolve in strong bases like an acidic nonmetal oxide, reacting with both.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Boron, the top element of Group 13, is a non-metal (a metalloid), whereas aluminium and the rest of the group are metals. Why is only the top element non-metallic?
_answer: Boron is very small with a high ionization energy, so it holds its electrons tightly and tends to share rather than lose them (non-metallic); going down the group, atoms get larger and ionization energy falls, so the elements become metallic.
_explanation: Metallic character depends on how easily electrons are lost. Boron's small size and high ionization energy make it cling to its electrons and bond covalently like a non-metal. Lower in the group the larger atoms release electrons more easily, so aluminium and its heavier congeners behave as metals.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Organic reagents are broadly classified as either 'electrophiles' or 'nucleophiles'. What fundamental property distinguishes these two kinds of reactive species?
_chapter: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
_answer: Electrophiles are electron-deficient species that seek electrons, while nucleophiles are electron-rich species that donate a pair of electrons; reactions occur when a nucleophile supplies electrons to an electrophile.
_explanation: The distinction is about electrons. An electrophile ('electron-loving') is short of electrons and attacks electron-rich sites, whereas a nucleophile ('nucleus-loving') has electrons to give and attacks electron-poor sites. Their complementary needs drive the bond formation in most organic reactions.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A covalent bond can break in two distinct ways — evenly, giving two neutral fragments, or unevenly, giving two oppositely charged fragments. What determines which type of bond breaking occurs?
_chapter: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
_answer: Even breaking (homolysis) gives free radicals and is favoured for nonpolar bonds under heat or light; uneven breaking (heterolysis) gives ions and is favoured for polar bonds in polar solvents that stabilize the resulting charges.
_explanation: How a bond breaks depends on the bond's polarity and the conditions. Nonpolar bonds tend to split their shared pair evenly into radicals (homolysis), especially with heat or light, while polar bonds break unevenly into ions (heterolysis) when a polar solvent can stabilize the separated charges.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A drop of ink or plant pigment placed on paper and touched with solvent separates into a series of coloured bands that travel different distances. How does this chromatography pull apart a mixture into its components?
_chapter: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
_answer: The components distribute themselves differently between a stationary phase (the paper) and a moving solvent (the mobile phase); those that cling less to the paper and dissolve more in the solvent travel farther, so the mixture separates into bands.
_explanation: Chromatography separates substances by their differing affinities for a fixed phase versus a flowing phase. Each component is carried along at a rate set by how strongly it is held by the stationary phase compared with how readily it moves with the solvent, so different substances end up at different positions.

subject: chemistry
question_text: The hydrogen atom in acetylene (HC≡CH) is weakly acidic and can be removed by a strong base, whereas the hydrogens in ethane cannot. Why is a hydrogen attached to a triple-bonded carbon acidic?
_chapter: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
_answer: The sp-hybridized carbon in acetylene has high s-character, so it holds bonding electrons closer to the nucleus and is effectively more electronegative; this stabilizes the negative charge of the carbanion left after removing the proton, making the C–H acidic.
_explanation: Acidity depends on how stable the anion is once the proton leaves. The sp carbon's greater s-character makes it more electronegative and better able to hold the extra electron pair, stabilizing the resulting carbanion. Ethane's sp³ carbons have less s-character, so their C–H bonds are not acidic.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Having alternating double bonds in a ring is not enough to make a molecule 'aromatic' and specially stable. What conditions must a ring actually satisfy to be aromatic?
_answer: The ring must be planar and cyclic with a continuous loop of delocalized p-electrons numbering (4n+2) — Hückel's rule; only then does it gain the special aromatic stability.
_explanation: Aromaticity requires more than alternating bonds: the molecule must be flat, have a closed loop of overlapping p-orbitals, and contain a specific number of delocalized electrons given by (4n+2). Benzene, with six such electrons in a planar ring, meets all these conditions, which is the source of its exceptional stability.

subject: chemistry
question_text: As you move from alkanes to alkenes to alkynes, the flame produced on burning becomes increasingly yellow and sooty. Why does greater unsaturation lead to a sootier flame?
_answer: More unsaturated hydrocarbons have a higher proportion of carbon relative to hydrogen, so their combustion is less complete and leaves unburnt carbon particles (soot), producing a yellow, smoky flame.
_explanation: A higher carbon-to-hydrogen ratio means more carbon must be oxidized, and with limited oxygen some remains unburnt as glowing soot. Alkynes and alkenes, being richer in carbon than alkanes, therefore burn with sootier, more luminous flames than the cleaner-burning saturated alkanes.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Ethane's two carbons can rotate freely about their single bond, yet the molecule spends most of its time in the 'staggered' arrangement rather than the 'eclipsed' one. Why does ethane prefer the staggered form?
_answer: In the staggered arrangement the C–H bonds on the two carbons are as far apart as possible, minimizing the repulsion (torsional strain) between their electron pairs, so it is the lower-energy, preferred conformation.
_explanation: Although rotation about the single bond is free, the different rotational positions have different energies. The eclipsed form brings C–H bonds on adjacent carbons directly in line, increasing electron-pair repulsion, while the staggered form spaces them out to reduce this strain, so ethane favours the staggered conformation.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Propene normally adds HBr according to Markovnikov's rule, but if a peroxide is present the bromine adds to the opposite carbon instead. Why does adding a peroxide reverse the outcome?
_answer: The peroxide triggers a free-radical mechanism instead of the usual ionic one; in the radical pathway the more stable carbon radical forms at the other carbon, so bromine ends up on the anti-Markovnikov position.
_explanation: Without peroxide, HBr adds through a carbocation, and the more stable cation dictates a Markovnikov product. Peroxides initiate a radical chain in which a bromine atom adds first, generating the more stable radical at the opposite carbon, so the final product has bromine on the anti-Markovnikov carbon (this effect is specific to HBr).

subject: chemistry
question_text: In close-packed arrangements of identical metal atoms, the spheres fill only about 74% of the available space at most — never the full 100%. Why can't identical spheres pack to fill all the space?
_answer: Rigid identical spheres inevitably leave empty gaps (voids) between them no matter how they are stacked; the densest possible arrangement (close packing) fills only about 74% of space, leaving the rest as interstitial voids.
_explanation: Spheres cannot deform to fill corners and gaps, so even the most efficient stacking leaves interstitial holes between them. The maximum packing efficiency for equal spheres is about 74%, which is why crystalline metals always contain some empty space in the form of tetrahedral and octahedral voids.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Some ionic crystals have ions genuinely missing from their proper lattice positions, yet the crystal as a whole stays electrically neutral. How can a crystal have vacancies and still be neutral?
_answer: In a Schottky defect, equal numbers of cation and anion vacancies occur together, so the missing positive and negative charges balance and the crystal remains electrically neutral overall.
_explanation: A crystal must stay neutral, so ions cannot simply vanish one type at a time. In the Schottky defect, a cation and an anion are missing in pairs, keeping the total positive and negative charge equal; this lowers the crystal's density but preserves its neutrality.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Heating colourless sodium chloride crystals in sodium vapour turns them yellow. What causes previously white crystals to become coloured?
_answer: The vapour drives a metal-excess defect: anion sites are left vacant and trap electrons (F-centres), and these trapped electrons absorb visible light, giving the crystal its yellow colour.
_explanation: Exposure to sodium vapour deposits extra sodium, leaving chloride-ion vacancies that capture electrons to maintain neutrality. These trapped electrons, called F-centres, absorb particular wavelengths of visible light, so the transmitted light appears coloured, turning the once-white crystal yellow.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Limp, wilted vegetables become crisp again when soaked in fresh water. What process draws water into the plant cells to firm them up?
_answer: Osmosis — water moves across the semipermeable cell membranes from the surrounding fresh water (low solute concentration) into the cells (higher solute concentration), swelling and stiffening them.
_explanation: Cell membranes let water pass but not the dissolved solutes. When wilted cells with concentrated contents are placed in fresh water, water flows in by osmosis to equalize concentrations, filling the cells and restoring their firmness — the same principle that dehydrates cells placed in strong salt solutions.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A mixture of ethanol and water cannot be separated into pure ethanol by ordinary distillation, no matter how carefully it is done. Why does distillation fail to give pure ethanol here?
_answer: Ethanol and water form an azeotrope — a mixture that boils at a constant temperature with the vapour having the same composition as the liquid — so distillation cannot change the composition beyond that point.
_explanation: Normally distillation works because vapour is richer in the more volatile component. But at the azeotropic composition the vapour and liquid have identical compositions, so boiling and condensing no longer enrich the mixture, and simple distillation cannot push past it to obtain pure ethanol.

subject: chemistry
question_text: One mole of sodium chloride lowers water's freezing point about twice as much as one mole of sugar does. Why does the salt have roughly double the effect of the sugar?
_answer: Sodium chloride dissociates into two ions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻) per formula unit, so it produces about twice as many dissolved particles as sugar, which stays as single molecules; colligative effects depend on the number of particles.
_explanation: Colligative properties like freezing-point depression scale with the number of dissolved particles, captured by the van't Hoff factor. Since salt splits into two ions while sugar remains one particle, a mole of salt releases roughly twice the particles, so it depresses the freezing point about twice as much.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Most solids dissolve better in hot water than in cold, but gases actually dissolve less as the water gets hotter. Why do solids and gases respond to temperature in opposite ways?
_answer: Dissolving most solids is endothermic, so heat drives it forward and raises solubility; dissolving gases is exothermic, so heating shifts the equilibrium to expel gas, lowering its solubility.
_explanation: By Le Chatelier's principle, adding heat favours the endothermic direction. Since dissolving a typical solid absorbs heat, warming helps it dissolve, whereas dissolving a gas releases heat, so warming pushes the gas back out of solution — which is why warm soda goes flat and warm water holds less dissolved oxygen.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A galvanic cell produces electricity all by itself, but electrolysis needs an external power supply to make it run. What is the fundamental difference between the two?
_answer: A galvanic cell runs a spontaneous reaction (negative ΔG) and produces electrical energy, whereas electrolysis forces a non-spontaneous reaction to occur by supplying electrical energy from an external source.
_explanation: The direction of the reaction distinguishes them. In a galvanic cell the chemistry naturally wants to proceed and releases energy as current, while in an electrolytic cell the desired reaction is uphill in free energy, so an outside power source must push electrons the 'wrong' way to make it happen.

subject: chemistry
question_text: When you dilute an electrolyte solution, its molar conductivity increases while its overall (specific) conductivity decreases. Why do these two measures move in opposite directions on dilution?
_concept: conductivity and molar conductivity on dilution
_answer: Dilution lets the ions dissociate and move more freely, raising the conductivity per mole (molar conductivity), but it also spreads fewer ions through each unit volume, lowering the conductivity of a given volume (specific conductivity).
_explanation: Molar conductivity considers all the ions from one mole of electrolyte, and dilution reduces inter-ionic interference so each mole conducts better. Specific conductivity, however, measures conduction per unit volume, and since dilution decreases the number of ions in that volume, it falls — hence the opposite trends.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Just by looking at a table of standard electrode potentials, a chemist can predict whether a given redox reaction will proceed on its own. How does the table reveal this?
_answer: You combine the half-cell potentials into a cell potential (E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode); if this comes out positive, the reaction is spontaneous, because a positive cell potential corresponds to a negative free-energy change.
_explanation: Electrode potentials rank how strongly species tend to gain electrons. Pairing the two relevant half-reactions and computing the overall cell potential tells you the driving force: a positive value means the reaction releases energy and occurs spontaneously, while a negative value means it does not without outside help.

subject: chemistry
question_text: An ordinary battery runs down and dies, but a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell can keep producing electricity indefinitely. Why doesn't the fuel cell run out the way a battery does?
_answer: A fuel cell's reactants (hydrogen and oxygen) are supplied continuously from outside rather than being stored inside, so as long as fuel keeps flowing the reaction — and the current — continues without the cell depleting itself.
_explanation: A battery stores a fixed amount of reactants internally and stops when they are used up. A fuel cell instead has its reactants fed in from external tanks, so it never exhausts its own contents; it produces electricity for as long as fuel and oxidant are supplied.

subject: chemistry
question_text: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gas can sit together indefinitely without reacting, yet a tiny spark makes it explode instantly. Why does a thermodynamically favourable reaction need a trigger to begin?
_answer: Although the reaction releases energy overall, it has a high activation energy barrier that the molecules cannot overcome at room temperature; the spark supplies the initial energy to start it, after which the heat released keeps it going.
_explanation: Thermodynamics tells us the reaction is favourable, but kinetics governs whether it actually proceeds. The mixture is stable because few molecules have enough energy to surmount the activation barrier; a spark gives some molecules that energy, and the energy they release then ignites the rest in a self-sustaining reaction.

subject: chemistry
question_text: For a first-order reaction, the time taken to use up half the reactant is the same whether you start with a large amount or a small amount. Why is the half-life independent of how much you begin with?
_answer: For a first-order reaction the rate is proportional to concentration, so the fraction reacting in a given time is constant; the half-life (0.693/k) depends only on the rate constant, not on the starting concentration.
_explanation: Because a first-order reaction slows in proportion to how much reactant remains, the same fraction always disappears in the same time. This makes the time to fall to half its value constant regardless of the initial amount, a defining and useful feature of first-order kinetics (as in radioactive decay).

subject: chemistry
question_text: The molecularity of a reaction step is always a whole number, but the experimentally measured reaction order can be fractional or even zero. Why can order take values that molecularity cannot?
_answer: Molecularity counts the actual molecules colliding in a single elementary step, which must be a whole number; order is an experimental quantity reflecting the overall multi-step mechanism, so it can come out fractional or zero.
_explanation: An elementary step involves a definite, countable number of molecules, so its molecularity is necessarily integral. Reaction order, by contrast, is determined by how rate depends on concentrations across the whole mechanism, which can produce non-integer or zero values that molecularity never can.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Even when reactant molecules collide with more than enough energy to react, many collisions still fail to produce any product. Besides sufficient energy, what else must be right for a collision to be effective?
_answer: The molecules must also collide with the correct orientation so that the reacting parts meet; a properly energetic but wrongly aligned collision does not lead to reaction.
_explanation: Collision theory requires both enough energy to overcome the activation barrier and a suitable geometry of approach. If molecules strike each other with the wrong parts facing, the necessary bonds cannot form even with ample energy, so only collisions that are both energetic and correctly oriented are effective.

subject: chemistry
question_text: When a gas is adsorbed on a solid, in some cases gentle warming easily reverses the process, while in others the gas is held so firmly it is essentially permanent. Why can adsorption be so weak in one case and so strong in another?
_answer: Weak, reversible adsorption (physisorption) is held only by van der Waals forces and is easily undone by warming; strong, often irreversible adsorption (chemisorption) involves actual chemical bonds between the gas and the surface.
_explanation: The two types differ in the nature of the attraction. Physisorption relies on feeble physical forces that heat easily overcomes, so it is reversible, whereas chemisorption forms genuine chemical bonds that are much stronger and typically require far more energy to break, making it essentially permanent.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Using the very same set of reactants, chemists can obtain different major products simply by choosing a different catalyst. How can changing only the catalyst change what product is formed?
_answer: Catalysts are selective — each one lowers the activation energy for a particular reaction pathway, so a given catalyst speeds up the route to one product while leaving others slow, steering the reactants toward a specific product.
_explanation: A catalyst does not change the thermodynamics but accelerates one route among several. By offering a low-energy path to a particular product, a specific catalyst makes that reaction dominate, so switching catalysts can direct the same starting materials toward entirely different products.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Adding a little electrolyte (salt) to a stable colloidal solution can make its particles clump together and settle out. Why does salt destabilize a colloid?
_answer: Colloidal particles carry like electric charges that keep them apart; the added ions neutralize these surface charges, removing the repulsion, so the particles collide, aggregate, and settle out (coagulation).
_explanation: A colloid is kept stable by the mutual repulsion of similarly charged particles. Introducing an electrolyte supplies oppositely charged ions that neutralize the particles' charge, allowing them to come together and grow heavy enough to settle, which is why salts coagulate colloids (as river silt settles where rivers meet the sea).

subject: chemistry
question_text: To concentrate a powdered sulfide ore, it is mixed with oil and water and air is blown through; the valuable ore floats off in the froth while the rocky impurity sinks. Why does the ore rise but the waste sink?
_chapter: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements
_answer: In froth flotation the sulfide ore particles are made water-repellent and cling to the oil-coated air bubbles, so they rise in the froth, while the water-wettable rocky gangue is not picked up and sinks.
